utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, along with Mr. Jim Cowles, an attorney from the United States who will be helping us in the absence of several of our other trial attorneys and Mr. Huber, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jim Cowles. It's an honour to be before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Welcome to the Tribunal. May we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic along with my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Niko Duric, attorney from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, and along with Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, I'm appearing on behalf of Mr. Hasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Mr. Esad Landzo, along with Nancy Boler from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly swear the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I do have about a 15-minute opening statement that I would like to make because we've never made one. I promise not to be as long as Mr. Ostberg or Mr. Tupuskovic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want to make an opening statement, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear him. Swear the witness first. Let him swear

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I promise not to belabour you with the legal submissions that we all submitted when the Prosecution closed its case, but I'd like to remind the court that all those legal submissions and issues have been carried through the Defence, all the way, Mucic, Delalic, Delic and Landzo intends to carry those legal issues all the way through the Defence case too. But, I come here this morning to speak to you only about the evidence that applies to Esad Landzo. I'm not going to address this court like I would an American jury because I'm not going to insult you that way, but this is the first assertion of an affirmative, special defence in an international criminal forum. It can not be viewed in a vacuum. You're not going to hear a fairytale from me, but you are going to hear about a young man from a small town of Konjic, a young Bosnian boy, who for all his life was basically forgotten. He was sickly. He couldn't go out and play with the other boys and play football. He was ostracised by his peers. His mother would send him to school with a warm towel soaked in goat's fat around his neck to try to help his rest respiratory problems. He became a loaner. He would prefer to stay with stray dogs in the woods than to associate with his peers. But, he had one thing that he excelled in, he was the best artist in his school. And the other children, when they wanted him to draw pictures, then they would want to talk to him. His teacher had this hope that one day he would go to art school and he would return to Konjic and he would replace her as the instructor for art in the Konjic schools. This boy was excepted to art school in Sarajevo and he attended art school for two weeks. Then his father explained to him that the family could not afford the bus tokens to go to Sarajevo and that he had to work and help support his father, his mother, and his four siblings and he had to drop out of art school. So he went to carpentry school, along with the other boys, even though the dust from the carpentry work adversely affected his breathing difficulties, and so he graduated with a carpentry degree and then he went to work for a young entrepreneur in town, as a guard in their warehouse. Then the shelling of Konjic began. Well, that young boy is now six years older, and I would like for Mr. Landzo, would you rise for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has said on a number of occasions through the Prosecution's case, let the victim tell his story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the true victim of the aggression in this case is Esad Landzo and all the Esad Landzos who, through this aggression, have lost their families, their friends, their communities, their dreams and their youth. Now the Trial Chamber has agreed to hear one more victim of this aggression. The evidence in this case, through the Prosecution and the Defence case, has shown that 20.000 to 30.000 refugees poured into the Konjic area in April and May of 1992. With each one of these refugees, came their stories of murder, rape, destruction, loss of homes and families, and as they came through, they told this story to Esad Landzo and all the other Esad Landzos in that community. They were apprised of what they thought would happen when the shelling of Konjic began. You add this atmosphere of panic and fear and anger to an already fragile unstable personality, and the evidence of the psychiatrists and psychologists that are going to testify in this case will explain the state of diminished mental responsibility that existed in Esad Landzo in 1992. This trial chamber has refused to define the Defence provided for in Rule 67 of the Rules of Procedure and has stated that the criteria to be applied will be clear in the verdict. The Defence is faced with the danger of putting on evidence that they have no idea what is really relevant to the Defence without a definition. The accused is exposed to the risk of a speculative trial, or worse, as stated in the Tadic case, that the perception could be that the Judges are working the other way around, that they come to guilt first and then they decide what the law is they will apply. The most commonly accepted doctrines on diminished responsibility are based in the English homicide act of 1957, although no definition has been provided for the Defence of what the Defence must prove to the Trial Chamber, this is the definition that is going to be relied on in asserting this Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Where a person kills or is a party to a killing of another, he shall not be convicted of murder if he was suffering from such an abnormality of mind, whether arising from a condition of a rested or retarded development of mind or any inherent causes or induced by disease or injury as substantially impaired his mental responsibility for his acts and omission in doing or being a party to the killing. The Defence evidence will show that one of the most horrendous experiences that any person could experience, happened to this 18-year-old boy. When he was 18, he and a friend tried to leave Konjic and find work in Croatia, and in the meantime, they were inducted into a Croatian military training facility where they not only were taught horrible murderous torturous kinds of killing by videotape, but while they were in this instruction room, a Serb woman was brought into the room and the proper way of slitting a throat was demonstrated in front of these young boys. This Trial Chamber must recognise that, in order to fulfil the burden of proving an accused suffered from diminished mental responsibility at the time of the allegations set forth in this indictment, all the evidence regarding his mental state at that time is relevant. Not only is the evidence relevant, but the succession of events leading to the fragile personality that existed in April, May, June, July of 1992 is relevant evidence. The scientific evidence is not a luxury for us. The case law says that in order to raise the defence, the scientific evidence must support the defence asserted. The scientific experts that are coming forward will describe various conditions, and these various conditions are a psychological condition called DMS-IV which includes personality disorders, schizoid personality disorder, antisocial personality disorder, narcissistic personality disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Because Esad Landzo existed in such a diminished mental capacity at that time, he was ripe for exploitation. He was exploited by the Croatians, by the Serbs, his own leaders, and by force of circumstance at the time. Our evidence will show that Esad Landzo was, since infancy, a very sick boy. He suffered from a very serious breathing problem with his asthma, and he could never go out and play with the other children. If he exerted himself he couldn't wreath. The evidence will show that he was involved in an incident in 1991 which severed the fourth and fifth digit of his right hand rendering those digits deformed and useless. This testimony will be supported by two Dutch doctors that will come testify. The Trial Chamber and the most of the rest of us have been here for going on two years, and the trial began on March 10, 1997. The Prosecution took one full year to present their case. We listened to the Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution witnesses came here to tell their stories. They had six years to prepare their stories. They moved on to different locations. They read about the charges. They saw Esad Landzo being arrested before the news, they read about the charges against him. They met with his --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I object? I don't believe this is opening statement. This is closing argument, discussing the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a Defence that we are relying on that because Esad Landzo was the only one here as a guard, the only person identifiable, that these Serb witnesses, these Prosecution witnesses tailored all their testimony to support the one person on trial here in The Hague and that's Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What the Prosecution did is not an opening speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What the Prosecution did before the indictment is not an opening speech. The opening speech leads to what evidence you lead in Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the evidence will show that because he was the only one here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Go on that line, what you will tell the Trial Chamber about the defence of Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Our evidence will show that, and I'm not going to walk over to the model right now, but, the Judges know that because Esad Landzo was stationed, most of the time as the guard in front of hangar number 6, the building where the majority of the Serb detainees were held, he was the only name they knew. When they needed contact with the outside world, everyone, the 250 detainees in that hangar, they sent their representatives to the door, and they said Esad Landzo, Zenga. He answered their calls for food. He answered their calls to solve their problems. He slept right there. He didn't sleep in the administration building with the rest of the guards. That little hole that you see, that dugout on the hill, right over hangar number 6 door, that's where Mr. Landzo stationed himself and he stayed there with his dog, that he took care of, there in Celebici. Because of that fact, he was the person most contacted. He became the symbol of everything that happened in that arena. He was the token guard, and the Serb witnesses tailored their testimony to fit the revenge they sought. I'm not going to go into any other political arguments right now, but the evidence will show that we have asserted two affirmative defences in this case. We believe that once this court listens to all the evidence and listens to this victim tell his story, that you will find, because he suffered such a diminished mental capacity and mental responsibility at that time, that Esad Landzo should be found not guilty of the charge of murder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may now lead your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I need to get one more book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. van Leeuwen; is that correct? Would you state your full name for the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second name, "van Leeuwen."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have had different pronunciations in this court today. But, I will try to use the correct one. I would like for you to -- can you tell the court how you first got involved in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the request of Mrs. Sampayo, of this Tribunal, to evaluate whether the accused's psychiatric condition was compatible with his confinement of the United Nations detention unit, and I made a report on 6 November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then you made subsequently three reports regarding Mr. Landzo. Can you tell the court what the issues were in each one of the three reports that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second one was the accused lacking mental responsibility or was he -- excuse me. The second one was, is the accused suffering from a mental disorder that renders him unable to understand and follow the proceedings against him and/or assist in his defence, and if so, please answer the following questions, but my answer was that he was not suffering from such a mental disorder that rendered him unable to understand it and so on. And I sent my -- I made my report at 25 November 1996. And the last one, that was the accused lacking mental responsibility or was he in a state of diminished mental responsibility at the time he was alleged to have committed the offence. The second question that the mental health of the accused at the time of the events in question affect his ability to understand the wrongfulness of his alleged conduct or influence that conduct and if so to what extent. And I sent my report at 13 January 1997. And then a couple of weeks ago, I think two to three weeks ago, you telephoned me, and you sent a fax and you said that I should be asked to come to the court to testify, and you asked me to see once more Mr. Landzo, and I thought that was a reasonable question because I hadn't seen him since January 1997, and I don't like to talk about a person whom I haven't seen for such a long time. So I spoke with Mr. Landzo last Sunday, not yesterday, but yesterday a week ago in the United Nations detention unit in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, I wanted to ask now -- Your Honours, these three reports that Dr. van Leeuwen previously made, discuss in detail some events that are relevant to Mr. Landzo's condition, and I would like to offer these three reports into evidence at this time. They are before the court anyway for other purposes, but I would like to offer them at this time as evidence relevant to Mr. Landzo's mental condition in 1992 because he goes back and he describes his family history, the history of school, and everything else that's relevant to the condition he ended up in in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Oppose of testing him at that time. It was not really turned back. You had what he read as to why he was testing him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But the facts in the report itself, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You heard what he read that was referred to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Will the court accept the third one that dealt with the mental responsibility of the defendant? That's exactly what he was trying to decide the issue in 1996. I'm offering then, if the court does not want to accept report 1 and 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nobody is denying that he examined the accused, but you're projecting it back to a period which was not in issue at that time. The reference to him stated whether he was capable of standing trial, whether his detention in the prisons there was compatible. And lastly, his diminished mental responsibility did not refer back to any dates. So you don't talk about a date reference back to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the third report dealing with his mental responsibility at the alleged time of the allegations in the indictment is precisely the Defence we're asserting, and I believe that every word that Dr. van Leeuwen wrote at that time is not only relevant, but it's mandatory to support exactly what Dr. van Leeuwen found in 1996 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see we're speaking at cross purposes. I'm not saying that you're not suggesting a defence of diminished responsibility. But when reference was made to the doctor, specific terms of reference was made to him, and that was what he determined in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, the Defence is offering the third report dealing with the mental responsibility of Mr. Landzo in 1992. Is that report going to be accepted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it refers to that, it will be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Is it accepted into evidence or is it just going to be taken into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, every report relating to mental capacity of accused persons will be accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is when you're making your statements, restrict yourself to the terms of reference to which the reference was made to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to now pass out a copy of that third report to the Trial Chamber for your reference while Dr. van Leeuwen is testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear, if we could just have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The third report is marked D46/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do the others have numbers also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Should have.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one is D44/4 and the second one, D45/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm still not clear. Does the court wish to receive the other two reports or not? I've passed out the third one which is dealing with mental responsibility in 1992, but the statements and the history of Mr. Landzo are included in D44/4 and D45/4, and would the court approve of considering these also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the doctor made three reports. I don't know which your last one is referring to, whether that is your own particular one. I knew the references to which the Trial Chamber, in consultation with the registrar, referred to him, and I think that is what he was speaking to, the last which you telephoned him and made your own private arrangement is quite different. So I don't know what has happened there, what he had already reported to the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecution, I think, has copies of those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, you submitted to me a curriculum vitae in Dutch, so I am not able to really read it myself, but I would just like to go through your training and your qualifications as an expert in forensic psychiatry today. Could you tell the court where you studied psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started medicine in Leiden University. Afterwards, I specialised in psychiatry at the Utrecht University and I got my Ph.D. degree at the Amsterdam University. Afterwards, I started to work for a mental hospital and for a community mental health centre. At that time, I wrote my -- I wrote a book for the -- I did a study for the PhD degree which was about emergency psychiatric. Besides, I did expert work since the beginning of the '70s for the court in Utrecht and after I moved to Maastricht where I worked for the mental hospital there. I kept my work for the Utrecht court in doing expertises in criminal law cases. Afterwards, Maastricht court asked me to do the same, and from the beginning of 1981, I started to work completely in forensic psychiatry, that's to say, I'm part-time working for the Ministry of Justice in Maastricht. That means being a consultant for the court and for the two detention units in remand houses and prisons in Maastricht and Sittard. Since 1986, I'm part-time professor in forensic psychiatry at the law school of Leiden University.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you've also attended different conferences in other countries too concerning forensic psychiatry, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What were those? What countries have you studied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I studied in the United States and several times in New York and Boston area, Washington. I was especially interested in the position of the expert in the adversarial system of the common law. I was interested in how do they deal with the issue of criminal responsibility, and I was interested in the shooing (phoen) area, how it worked out with psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you reviewed the law that I submitted to the Trial Chamber as the law that is most commonly used in the international community in reference to diminished mental responsibility, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think, to my opinion, I'm a clinician, I need to do my own work, and I need to present my knowledge, my conclusions, but they are always clinical. But I need to make them that they are understandable for lawyers, because the lawyers, they need to do the work in a courtroom. I think the international opinion is always the same, that if you talk about criminal responsibility, first of all you need to detect whether there is a disorder or not at the time of the alleged conduct. That's the first thing. Afterwards, you need to evaluate whether there is a linkage between this disorder and that conduct. If so, how do you evaluate that, because for every conduct, you need, first of all, to be conscious of your own behaviour. Second, you need to have insight in the consequences of your act, consequences in the field of criminal law too; and third, you need to make a decision that has to do with your willingness or not. We know that mental disorders can influence those three mental functions, and by evaluating that in that way, you can say there is some kind of diminished criminal responsibility or maybe there is no criminal responsibility. I think that is the other rule, we call it other rule, that started with the American Law Association, and that is internationally recognised and was the formulation in -- I got from Ms. Sampayo too. To understand the wrongfulness of his alleged conduct or influence of that conduct and if so to what extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That definition that Madam De Sampayo gave you differs from the definition that we're using for diminished mental capacity in this courtroom, in fact, that definition that Madam De Sampayo gave you to utilise as the standard that you were to apply is really the Dutch standard, and that has nothing to do with diminished responsibility. That has to do with lack of responsibility; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I impose an objection at this point. I don't believe the Trial Chamber has ruled as to a legal definition at this time. So whether counsel has provided different national laws on the definition of diminished responsibility to this doctor is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you might be later on, the Trial Chamber is not to rule until it knows what are the concentrations of the Defence. We do not yet know what the Defence is about. Until we know what it is and what the Defence relies upon, you are free to question the way you are going.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, as a forensic psychiatrist, Dr. van Leeuwen, you can make a clinical evaluation as far as psychiatry goes of Mr. Landzo, but without a definition, you can't come to any forensic criminal conclusion, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think a criminal conclusion, I don't need to make. That's the lawyer's work. I can only make my clinical conclusions, but I do agree with you that if I say to the court, "This man is suffering from that mental disorder," and then finished, then I shouldn't be a forensic psychiatrist. So I need to do some translation, and that we have the word of the criminal responsibility. That's the translation between the clinical conclusions on the one side, and the work of the court on the other side presenting a verdict.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, counsel, what you have invited the expert to tell the Trial Chamber is a state of mind of the accused person at the time he committed the offence. He is not expected to go into the legal arguments about conduct, omission or anything of that nature. He is to tell us what the mental state is, and within the definition which we are going about abnormality of mind, whether it arose from inherent causes or whether it is from arrested or retarded development of mind. These are the things he is expected to tell us. He is not expected to tell us what the legal definition is. The legal definition rests with the Trial Chamber in determining the extent of what counsel has established before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that's absolutely right. My only concern is that he will testify about the mental state of Mr. Landzo in 1992, but as an expert, an expert can be asked to form an opinion on an ultimate issue in the case. In order for him to form an opinion, we're just trying to come up with an assumption of the law that we're using, and the court has just reconfirmed the fact that we are talking about the same premise of diminished responsibility. So I won't go into that anymore, but in order for him to come to a conclusion, he has to sate what standard he's applying, and that's why I was covering that with him. I'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may be careful to know that he is not a lawyer, and he's only using his medical knowledge to tell you what abnormality of mind is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's a forensic psychiatrist, though, and that's the difference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has explained to you already he was not giving you legal conclusions. He was not doing that. He told you that, right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, okay. I will be asking him legal conclusions later, but not until his mental state has been developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, can you describe to the court your contact with Esad Landzo, how you met him and how much time you spent with him and what the quality of the time was you spent with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first two evaluations, I spoke with him -- the first time I spoke for two and a half hours, and the second time was about five hours, and the last time, the last examination, I spoke with him about nine hours, and I say so because the first -- for the first report, I spoke once with him. For the second, I spoke twice with him. For the third one, I spoke three times with him. I think the first conversations were useful for the clinical evaluation too. And then last Sunday, I spoke with him for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In coming to your opinions about Mr. Landzo's mental state, were you provided other documents that you reviewed and took into consideration, his prior statements, prior statements of other psychiatrists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw -- I read the psychological expertise of Mrs. De Manredi (phoen), from Professor Lagazzi, and from Professor Loga.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you also provided a copy of the results from Dr. Alfredo Verde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Who is another clinical psychiatrist. With the assistance of the usher, I would like to ask now that this book be shown to Dr. van Leeuwen. I'll give you an excerpt from the book afterwards. Dr. van Leeuwen, do you recognise this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Who are the authors of this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is absolutely the internationally recognised standard work in the field of psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What is the title of the book and who are the authors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many authors. "Synopsis of Psychiatry, Behaviour Sciences/Clinical Psychiatry." There are many authors, but especially Mr. Kaplan and Mr. Sadock are the authors, but it is written by many, many, many, persons. It was absolutely outstanding work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that book is relied upon as authoritative by every psychiatrist in the international community, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'd like the -- with the assistance of the usher, would you provide Dr. van Leeuwen with these two copies? I think they have previously been marked, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have a copy here for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, the typed-out page right there that says "personality disorders," the first one? Do you recognise that as an exact definition from DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is this the definition that you rely on in making your evaluations each day when you evaluate clients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that definition as authoritative in the psychiatric field. It's the precursor. I'm sorry. I will get that. Dr. van Leeuwen, a person has to be determined to have a personality disorder under DSM-IV before he can go to the next table to determine what personality disorder exists; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, DSM-IV has been developed by the American Psychiatric Association, I believe, since '98, it was, and about two to three years ago, we got a fourth edition. What is DSM-IV? It has become the international bible for psychiatry, and just a matter to work, that you can work together and that you can communicate and do psychiatric research. It is a descriptive way of diagnosis. You describe symptoms. You describe behaviours. You don't talk about causes. And then second -- so it is a descriptive system and it's a categorical system, and it is a system with five axis. The first axis reveals the actual mental state, any kind of mental disorder. The second axis is their personality disorder. The DSM-IV gives for the axis to give the general -- can make general characteristics of a personality disorder, and then afterwards the categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the second paper that I've handed you which has categories of a table taken from -- is that table taken exactly from the book that is in front of you by Kaplan and Sadock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are these the criteria that are used as standards in the psychiatric field all over in the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so, and I can assure so that I do so and my colleagues in Holland do so. I'm using this everyday, several times, because every inmate I see for the first time, I need to write down the diagnosis, and I always do according to this system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are these pages exact copies from the pages that are inside that book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to introduce into evidence the criteria that all international psychiatry uses in determining, first, the personality disorder under DSM-IV and then the axis two criteria which is the second copied page out of the text which shows what personality disorders are to be determined. I'd like to introduce those into evidence to assist the court. The Prosecution has copies of these also.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection, except that D47/4 is the one piece of paper. It has no indication of from where it came within the larger book or what the page number or the source is or where it can be found. I don't know how it is excerpted from the larger book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will provide the Prosecution with the exact page at the next break, but it was the exact definition they use out of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would sure appreciate a copy of these exhibits if I could be provided with them at some point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think I may have extra copies right there if the usher would provide the Defence counsel with them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Once we have those identifications, we have no objection to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to offer it into evidence subject to my giving the Prosecution the exact page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think in trying to tender this, I think the sufficient identification should have been made as to its source. There's nothing here indicates how you got it or what it relates to and the authority for making it. It could well be your own creation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the expert witness if he identified that as the exact definition that he relies upon everyday, and he said it was, so, I believe that is authentication enough in the international community that it came from the definiton they use every single day to evaluate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nothing stops him from taking it and defining this as his own criteria. And then you do not rely on this piece of paper to be his own. But when you bring this piece of paper as nothing linking it with anything which is known to anyone else, I think it's fairly difficult to accept it as authority for what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the break, I will provide the exact page number in the book and re-offer that document into evidence, but I'd like for the court to be able to use it right now as reference during his testimony, and I'll re-urge the offering into evidence at another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He's still giving evidence, and he may be cross-examined on it, so you don't have to worry about the court using anything at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, you've explained what DMS-IV is. But can you explain to the court what is the standard in psychiatry that is used that is called reasonable psychiatric probability, and if you use that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that psychiatry has always used the word "probability" because it is not like -- it is not a natural signs of mental diseases, but we are making improvements to prove that many mental conditions has to do with biological factors. But we don't know -- still we don't know -- we don't know very much about mental functioning. So we need to work with probability. A human being is very complicated. Somebody's behaviour is a product of maybe endless number of factors, so we can always -- we can only analyse some of these factors, and I think that probability is the only reasonable word and the only word which is reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say "reasonable psychiatric probability," does that mean that it's more likely than not, that it occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it's based upon clinical evidence and the actual -- the state of art of our science.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Speaking of all of the things that add up to a decision for a mental psychiatric probability, I would like for you, however you want to use, if you would like to use the flip chart, to discuss what evidence is relevant, in approaching 1992, the mental state of Mr. Landzo at Celebici. If I might, if you would like to use -- oh, you have your own. Thank you. If you would like to use the flip chart or if you would just discuss with the court, in determining the mental state of someone at a set time on a timeline, what evidence is relevant in determining that state that existed at a set time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to use this, because I want to make clear one thing. We have mental diseases which come from nowhere. For example, we know a bit about it, but it seems that it comes from no where. A lot of the fields of psychiatry is what we call reactions. Do you understand reactions? And if you talk about reactions, and we think many diseases are to -- somatic diseases too are a matter of reaction. For example, you got an infection and your body is reacting. So if you talk about the mental state, we have circumstances, events, and they may be stressful. Can you read this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So circumstances, they are more prolonged, they are a bit lasting. Events are just for a moment. They may be stressful. For example, a war is a stressful circumstance, and in a war you can have stressful events. Then we have a person, and if we talk about the personality disorder, it is not something like being mad or being foolish, it is a person, you talk about a person, and every person has its characteristics. Every person can be vulnerable, but a person with a personality disorder is very much vulnerable in the conditions, even in the conditions in the culture where he is living. So you can be vulnerable in a specific way. What can happen is that special circumstances or events just trigger the person's vulnerability. You can have another person who is not very much vulnerable or the circumstances can not be triggering for the person. Then in the field of reactions, "reactions". The first responsibility is that the event. You have the circumstances of the event and you go on feeling adaptation or adjustment. The second possibility is that you can't adjust because of this. And the first possibility is what we call an acute stress disorder. That's more in the beginning. You have symptoms. For example, adaptation is not a thing which happens in one second. Everyone has stressful events. Sometimes you sleep for one night, you don't sleep very well, or that day you don't like your food. That has nothing to do with disease. But in acute stress disorder, you lose your self-control. You have not a feeling to be who you are. You are very unstable and you are crying, you are in a panic, you don't sleep, you don't like your food and like that for a couple of weeks. That's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, would you tell the court the difference between acute and chronic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the second possibility in adaptation is what's called in the DSM-IV is an adjustment disorder. That hasn't to do only with a war, for example, that has to do with normal life. Someone who comes to work very hard for 10, 20 years, there is a change and he can't adjust to the new circumstance and then he develops symptoms. You see, adjustment disorder means that you can't adapt anymore and you start to produce symptoms and those symptoms can be in the field of a depressive mood. It can be in a field of feeling yourself anxious, uncertain, you don't know what to do. You have lost all your self-control. It can be under the field of behaviour. You are doing things you would normally not do. The most specified is what is called the post-traumatic stress disorder. This is a special one because then you need to have suffered from very traumatic, not only stressful, but a very traumatic event which can give you the feeling to be very lonesome and very powerless. You are under the influence of a huge power which was overwhelming for you. Then usually there's a silent period. This is acute. This is immediately afterwards. This goes slowly -- not slowly, but it comes. There's always a linkage, somebody feels the linkage between this and this. This comes later. If I talk about Mr. Landzo, then here in this field, I think I can link my three things. First of all, I need to stress that when I talked with him for my report in January 1997, he was denying everything. So I couldn't ask him why did you do this? Why did you do that? Because he said, I didn't do those things. When I talked with him last Sunday, his mental condition had changed tremendously. It was absolutely amazing for me. It was like somebody else. He wasn't depressive anymore, and he was talking English fluently, and he couldn't talk any English when I spoke with him last year in January. He told me, as a psychiatrist, I was rather amazed, I said "You have changed." He said, "Yes, it's true. I feel much better," and so on. So he talked to me. He has a very good contact with his Defence counsel. She gave him the advice to learn English, and he did so, and he discovered that he was able to learn English. He was listening to the radio and so on. She got him a laptop so he got used a bit to work with the computer. But next to that, beside that, he talks twice a week with the Dutch psychiatrist, a psychologist who specialised in people who have suffered from a traumatic event. In total, once a month there's a psychiatrist from Luxembourg who is talking with him and that's a psychiatrist of Bosnian origin. But for him, he told me that it's more important that the Dutch psychologist will talk with him twice a week. Then, now he said to me, in the psychotherapy, I have made the decision to tell the truth. Now, I need to emphasise that I'm a psychiatrist, so it is not my job to evaluate whether somebody is telling the truth or not. That's your job. Let me be very clear on that. So I can only describe what he told me, and it had nothing to do with whether that is true or not. I can only work with what somebody is telling me. That doesn't mean anything about is this truthful or not. Anyway, he told me and told me what he did. He told me about Celebici, and he told me that he beat one man, he told me why he did so, and he told me how that man died from it. He told me another thing. He said to me that when I had the conversations with him for the three earlier reports, he regret very much that he couldn't talk with me freely. And now he told me that in those days, he had a Bosnian counsellor, Defence counsellor, who strictly advised him to deny and so he did so. I'm a psychiatrist, and I have had a lot of experience, I felt that he was very much willing to talk with me at that time. He was looking for it but, I as a psychiatrist, I had to respect his position of an accused who is denying. I felt that he was -- I was sure he has a story, but he is not allowed to talk about it. So now he did so. Now, for me, I have more possibilities to evaluate, to reconstruct his mental condition at the time of May 1992 in Celebici. First of all, the person of Mr. Landzo, from the beginning, many things went wrong. I think the Defence counsel has described it for you, so I'm not going to repeat it. But -- and you can read it in my report of January 1997. I still stick to it. So he has a personality disorder, but no, it's more obvious that that is a mixed personality disorder. We mean it is not one category. You need to use more categories to describe the reality of this person. One category is, he is lacking self-esteem, self-image. He cannot feel himself being a person, a human being. He has a lack of that. And that we call a borderline personality traits. Because of that, in relations, he can see through it, and it's very important because he is so empty to a certain extent, he can be very dependent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, I just want to interrupt you for a second. Those borderline and schizoid and dependant personalities, those are recognisable personality disorders on the chart that we have before the Trial Chamber, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, let me explain this. You see, this person, how dependent he is, he told me that in that camp, he was under the influence of a Mr. Delic. I don't know him so I just described what he told me. And he explained to me why he was under the influence of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Doctor, just one second. Your Honour, I'm going to object to any mention of my client and if they are getting into anything about my client, I will renew my motion to sever us from the Landzo Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think he's referring to other persons, and he's not even giving any evidence of what he told him. He should not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I ask that he be instructed to not give any evidence about what he was told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm only talking in clinical terms. I have nothing to do with guilt. That's not my job. I think that's very important to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's not what you mean. You are merely telling how he related to you. You are not telling the Tribunal what he told you, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not telling the Tribunal the details of what he told you, but how he related it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me about the relationship. It has nothing to do with the responsibility --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the doctor please use a microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to prove that that was the reality at that moment. I can tell you -- I can tell you one thing. He is a man who is very vulnerable for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I can't hear at all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. van Leeuwen. The interpretation booth says that they can't hear you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Use your earphones in case they might say anything you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Because this is clear, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if you talk about the dependency traits in Mr. Landzo's character, it is fascinating to see how he has changed. First, he had a lawyer, and his lawyer said to him, "You need to deny," and he did so, but he was totally willing to do something else, but that was impossible for him. And now, the influence, for example, of other persons, when he was 16, 17, it was his older brother who had to fill his life in offence of his brother. He couldn't make it himself. He couldn't make his own choices. Then in that camp, he said he was very much under the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You don't say what he told you, just his personal relationship with you should be enough. Don't say anything about anything that is happening here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It will help if you don't say the name of the person. You can say he was under the influence of another person. That probably would help if he doesn't name anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, he shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's kind of like trying to unring the bell. The bell has been rung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No. I think it will not be in the record. It should be redacted. He shouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anyhow, I need to have the possibility to talk about interactions and relationships to tell you the mental truth, you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whatever you use in coming to your conclusion will be sufficient for the Trial Chamber, but not the names of persons who he told you, because that might be against the rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I right if I use as a word, the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nothing like that. If he is the under the influence of anyone whatsoever, you can say he had some persons influencing him. Persons influencing him might be somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Might I suggest the person who represented authority or a superior? I think that would probably work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We would object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It would not be fair to name the co-accused person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry will be very happy with this claim. You can use it for corroborated evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is all the things which he has told the expert in confidential, and they should not be divulged here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to remind the court we asked for a severance two times, and in my Pre-Trial brief to the court in February of 1997, the possibility of this conflict arising came because the experts need to be able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We aren't going into the issues of severances or not. The Trial Chamber has ruled on that. It has to be a joint trial. When he comes to give his evidence, he can come to say anything and then the court will determine whether it can be taken into evidence. It is not for the expert who listened to him in confidence to come and tell the Trial Chamber what he told him. He's not giving evidence on behalf of him, or should he do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may be heard just for one minute? Your Honour, the Prosecution would, consistent with what Your Honours said, would agree, and I think this doctor has already said it, that what Mr. Landzo told this person is not being used for the truth of the matter, so both with respect to what Mr. Landzo said about himself, and even about others, we wouldn't -- I don't see Defence counsel suggesting that it's truth of the matter asserted. In fact, with respect to certain assumptions, she may well be having to bring in additional evidence to show that, in fact, some of it is true or not true. We would certainly agree that whatever Mr. Landzo told this person or the other persons is not admissible evidence against the other accused, if that will help things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose counsel should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is not on. I couldn't hear you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does this clear up the position as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, Your Honour. It just doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that whatever the accused told the expert in his examination of him is not evidence in this Trial Chamber and should not be mentioned for the purposes of his defence. He could have relied on him for making his conclusions, but definitely it has nothing to do with the evidence he is giving here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I take it then that Your Honours, if anything comes in, Your Honours will treat it like the court has already decided to treat the defendants custodial statements as not admissible against the other defendants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And totally irrelevant as to those defendants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not real happy about that, but I guess it's as happy as you're going to make me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely that is a loss, I know it, and accepting other circumstances where he comes in and observes other statements he made, that is a different matter. But when he wants to see through some of that, it couldn't be evidence before the Trial Chamber and will not be admitted. And we will not allow counsel to suggest it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just watch and see how things proceed, and if I need to make an objection, I will object. The court knows I'm not too shy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We also would protect other accused persons from such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and the court has been very good about that for this entire trial, and I'll protect my client and I'm sure the court will help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarity, if I might ask so that Dr. van Leeuwen is clear also, and that the Defence is clear, the statements of the accused to Dr. van Leeuwen are instrumental and necessary in his evaluation of the mental state of Mr. Landzo, but they have nothing to do with the truth of the matter asserted as against the other co-defendants, but it's relevant to the mental state, and he can discuss the relationships in generic terms. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, I'd like for you to look at your report that you submitted, the last one on mental responsibility, and in that report, I want you to describe to the court what evidence is relevant or all of the evidence that is relevant from the time Mr. Landzo was born until the time he appeared in Celebici in 1992. Would that be an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that has to do with personality disorder. It starts from, let's say, from the birth and even before that. We think. So that's very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: All of that evidence would be relevant to establishing his mental deficiency or mental responsibility at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is relevant but it's not the only relevant factor, and then I repeat what I wrote down here. In his case, the circumstances were the war, but so was everyone in that area had to do with it. Then you had his special experience in that correction camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you describe for the court what happened to Mr. Landzo, what the traumatic experience was in that Croatian camp? What I argued in opening statement is not evidence. If you can reflect what it was that occurred -- that happened to Mr. Landzo in that Croatian camp in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean what he was told happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I think he already qualified that the truth what was told to him but he used it to evaluate his conclusions. I'm asking him, that traumatic experience, if he could describe that to the court as explained to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't talk very much about it, just briefly. He told me what he saw there, what he saw where people were killed, tortured and so on. And it was one of those horrendous histories you heard from that area. He told me, the war will come in Bosnia too and you will see the same things, and that made him afraid. This is still, I think, in the field of normality, I think everyone would be shocked if he would get that information. Then he told me he saw on television the cruel things which happened in Croatia, and then it was started in Bosnia, and he was thinking about -- he told me he was thinking about rape and he was imagining that it would be just horrible if they would rape my 15-year-old sister. So I need to defend my family, and the only way to do so is to enter the army. Normal things. I mean, we all can understand this, but then he comes in the army, and he was not a mature person. He didn't have much reserves, do you use that, mental reserves, and that made him vulnerable. And then to a certain extent, the army was an attraction for him. I described it in my report what made it attractive for him, not in the field of logical thinking, but in the field of just his vulnerability and that was his dependency. So he is a man who can lose any possibility to make his own decisions and to make his own joy in a situation of dependency. And what he told -- let's say you have generals, you have soldiers, you have an army, but they keep their own personality. They make the choices, they make the decisions, they suffer but they don't change as a person. But he was. He was in the field of the adjustment disorder. He had the symptoms of it. He slept very badly. He told me he was using sleeping pills. He drank quite a lot and he combined it with the drug Akineton to have more affect over the alcohol. So he was not in a stable, mental condition at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So even in 1992, he was experiencing sleeping problems that he described to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back further in the life of Esad Landzo and can you describe the kind of isolated, lonely person he was in his childhood, if you could describe that for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you described it very well. I can't improve upon it. It's absolutely the same things I heard, and I wrote them in my third report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, what I say is not evidence in the courtroom. What you say is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I make it my evidence because this is absolutely true. For me, he was a boy playing alone in the woods with his dogs, and not just a regular dog, but dogs who were without a boss, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Stray dogs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stray dogs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I think you recounted that he also would adopt dogs who would have puppies? What would he do? What was his behaviour when he would have the dogs with the puppies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't talk very special about it. You see, there is always a combination of factors. Somebody who loves dogs doesn't me he has a personality disorder, but what made it in his case a presymptom of a later personality disorder is that he had only -- his only friends were dogs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All this information is based upon what Landzo himself told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually it is, because somebody -- let's say when I do an evaluation here in Holland, then a social worker can go to the family and talk, "What do you think about this person," and then you get more information that I didn't have in this case. It wasn't possible. So I can only give you the history, and then all of this should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You did not verify from any other source what he was saying to you was true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could follow the picture. I made my picture from what he told me, and that's -- I could work with it, but it's always the same, and I will repeat again, I just tell you what I heard and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: From his mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's the finish of my work. And I do the clinical interpretations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, can you tell the court what impact the fact that Mr. Landzo was not able to go to art school had on his future and his mental state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a rather complicated person. He is more complicated than I thought he would be. I thought in the beginning. For example, I saw poems he made. He is much more sensible, sensitive than you would imagine him to be. I wrote in my third report, I noted that he said "Bullets don't have eyes" as an expression, it is rather sophisticated, so I can't imagine that the reality of his life was poverty, and not many chances in the artistic fields. It is probably a field of his natural capacities, so that would have given him the possibility to develop a future for him. I think that's the same why his mental condition has improved nowadays, because now he has, again, hope for his future, because he learned English and he is now feeling with English you can build up a future for yourself. I think that was a disaster for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Before Mr. Landzo got to Celebici in 1992, can you describe the personality disorders that he suffered before he ever got to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did so. What I mentioned on the mixed personality disorder, and I meant borderline and dependent traits, characteristics, and then without a war, we don't know how he would have developed. Maybe he would have become an alcoholic person. For example, if he would have been able to finish that school, that would have compensated -- could have compensated his vulnerabilities in a way which is adequate from a societal point of view, adequate for society. But we don't know. To a certain extent, the war was fulfilling some of his shortnesses, his shortness in self-confidence, shortness of personality. So he had some kind of identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say he had some kind of identity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- in the war --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he was suffering from a lack of only identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Since he didn't have his own identity, the war gave him a temporary identity; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to the events in 1992 at Celebici. I believe that Mr. Landzo described to you events leading up to the beating of an old man. One of those, there was an event in July of 1992 when nine military police were killed outside of a small town named Bradina. Can you describe this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't describe the event. I can only describe what Mr. Landzo told me about it, and he told me that -- we had the same story, that he saw what happened in that little village, and he told me there was one man killed in a very cruel way, and that man used to be his neighbour, and he had a very good relationship with that man. So he was deeply shocked. That, I can understand, but I think a natural person would find a way to adapt to this very stressful event, but he used his reserves. That I can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because he had an adjustment disorder, he was unable to adapt like a normal person would have adapted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were aware that after he left Celebici he was transferred to Musala prison as a guard. Can you describe the contrast in the way he reacted at Musala prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I can only describe what he told me, and it was new for me, that he had worked in another camp too, and he said to me that was a normal camp with a normal commander. I asked him, are you alleged for misconduct in that camp too by the Tribunal? And he said, no, I'm not, it was a normal camp. He told me that there were prisoners in Musala who knew him from Celebici, and they said to him, "You are completely a different person," and therefore I just repeat, I tell you what he told me, but then my interpretation is that this story, if it is true, then it's -- it makes clear again the importance of the influential factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Of his dependant personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In combination with this disorder, if he has the right camp, the right commander, he does do what his commands are, and that is because -- he isn't his own person who reflects and says yes or no. He is unable to do so anyhow, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'm about to change topics. Would this be an appropriate time for us to take our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We would normally have taken a break at 11.30 and come back. Do you want to continue with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I only have maybe 15 or 20 more minutes with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honours, would that require a response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What response do you expect? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, I would like to ask you what your clinical conclusion would be as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My clinical conclusion is that Mr. Landzo is suffering from mixed personality disorder, together with borderline and especially dependent traits. So he is suffering from a lack of mental capacity, because that is the international recognised forensic psychiatric equivalent of the clinical judgment of a personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second, if I combine the information he gave to me, and that has nothing to do with whether it was true or not, but if I combine his information, as I described it here shortly, with my clinical conclusions, then I conclude that he was suffering from a mental disorder at the time of the alleged facts. According to the criteria of the DSM-IV, you can describe it as an adjustment disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the personality disorders that you just described, are they considered in psychiatric circles as abnormalities of the mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you can say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This mixed personality disorder that you described, did Mr. Landzo have the ability to exercise his own free will as a guard in Celebici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The personality disorder in itself can never explain a loss of capacity to exercise your own free will, because a personality disorder is a stable condition, a continuous condition. Therefore, I will repeat what I wrote down there. You can say in the case of Mr. Landzo that because of the interference of his personality disorder with all the vulnerability that is linked to it on the one side, and the special circumstances, the special events I mentioned, from a clinical point of view, the factor of an interpersonal influence, if it will prove to be true, is clinically of great importance, then he was in a condition, a mental condition, that he had a diminished capacity to exercise his own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What is your conclusion, your forensic conclusion, as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The consequence of a clinical conclusion that somebody was in a mental condition which diminished his capacity to exercise his own free will, from a forensic psychiatric point of view, my advice would be to consider him to have diminished responsibility at that time and for the acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. van Leeuwen. At this point, Your Honours, I would like to move to introduce the chart that Dr. van Leeuwen used to explain the conditions into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do I understand what you have applied for?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That sheet that Dr. van Leeuwen drew on which explains how he analysed the conditions, I would like to move that it's admitted into evidence. That just means it will go with the papers of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has a full report on the accused person. I don't see how this makes much of a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't hear any objection from the Prosecution that it be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not necessary. There is a full report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Delalic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of the second accused, Mr. Zdravko Mucic, has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. My name is Tom Moran, and I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I'm going to ask you some questions concerning the testimony you gave. I understand that English is not your native language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Frankly, sometimes I think English is not my native language because I ask questions that aren't very clear. Sometimes I let my mind overrun my mouth, if you would. If there is something that I ask you, and you don't understand the question or you're unclear about what I'm looking for, will you stop me, and I'll rephrase it, and we will work it out until we both understand it, so that I understand what I'm asking and you understand what you're answering. Can we do that? Now, one other thing, you have been real good during direct, but during cross-examination, I'm going to ask you to do this: If you look behind you, there is a lady with a funny machine behind you, and there's another one over there. They are court reporters, and they write down everything you say. They can't write down the nod you just gave me for a "yes." So you have to say "yes" or "no" if "yes" or "no" is appropriate. Will you do that for me, Doctor? See, Doctor, you're nodding again. You have to say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Finally, if the questions I ask call for a "yes" or "no" answer, will you just give me a "yes" or a "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You ask the question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: First thing is, you're both a physician and a Ph.D.; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you took your training as a physician, you took the same kinds of training that any other physician would take, infectious diseases, just regular physicians training, followed by some period of time as a resident in psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then after you became qualified as a psychiatrist, you went back and got a Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that's a different system in Holland than in the U.S.A. I don't know how it is in the U.S.A. But in Holland, if you pass a university degree that we call the doctorandus, then you pass a university -- you have a university degree. And only if you do a study and you describe it, we call that something like a thesis, and you have to defend it at the university, then you get a Ph.D. degree, and that's quite a job in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Getting a Ph.D. is quite a job anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, in Belgium, it is completely different, but that is the system in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you testified on direct that you met with Mr. Landzo a week ago Sunday. Did you prepare a report for anyone based on that meeting, a written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I got a map with interviews which had been taken in June '96. I read them briefly because I soon reached the conclusion that it was not interesting for my evaluations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's a question I asked wrong, so let me try it again. After you met with Mr. Landzo a week ago Sunday, did you prepare a written report of your conclusions based on that meeting a week ago Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. Thank you, Doctor. Doctor, you've talked about a thing called DSM-IV. All we've ever said is "DSM-IV." That's it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's part of that book, just a short part of it, but it is part of that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just so that everybody knows what "DSM-IV" stands for, it's the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, prepared by the American Psychiatric Association; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This thing is pretty much the bible worldwide on diagnosing mental disorders, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, so the Judges who may or may not be familiar with this thing, it has codes for various diseases, mental disorders, so that if you send a report to a doctor in England, he knows what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It sets out various criteria to determine whether or not someone is suffering from mental disorders ranging from mild depression through schizophrenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
