utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It sets these out in five axes; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You talked about the first two. The first axis is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It describes the actual mental condition. In the case of Mr. Landzo, I mentioned the adjustment disorder. That is an axis 1 disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Axis 2 is personality disorders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be something, for instance, like anti-social personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's one of the categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Axis 3 has to do with medical condition, physical medical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Whether he has pneumonia or diabetes or a broken leg or whatever; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Axis 4 has to do with any special conditions. For instance, a special condition axis 4 might be being incarcerated in the U.N. detention centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then axis 5 is a general look at his ability to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's measured on a scale of 0 to 100, isn't it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: At 100, somebody is -- I don't want to use the words "perfectly sane," because I don't think anybody is perfectly sane, but they are functioning just great in society, and zero would be just the opposite of that; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Landzo in November, the first time you met with him in November of 1996, did you arrive at a conclusion as to axis 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't try because I thought it wasn't relevant for the questions I had to answer at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about when you met with him later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about when you met with him in January of 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same answer. Because in the forensic psychiatric evaluation, you have to answer the question of criminal responsibility. In Holland, we have to give advice to the court how to go on with this fellow within the framework of criminal law. So axis 5 usually is not so important for that question. Secondly, with Mr. Landzo, about what period do you talk about? Because usually they say you reconstruct the axis 5 number from the last year, how was somebody functioning the last year. But Mr. Landzo spent most of that last year in prisons. So it was senseless to try to reconstruct axis 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So it makes no difference to anyone whether or not he is -- well, let me just go to the examples that are given in the DSM on what an axis 5 might be. I will just pick two of them at random directly out. Number 30, "Behaviour is considerably influenced by delusions or hallucinations or serious impairment of communications or judgment or inability to function in all areas," and compare that with code 100, which would be superior functioning in a wide range of activities. It would make no difference to a court where a defendant fit on that kind of scale? Is that what you're saying, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That depends. Because, for example, if I say to a court, "He scores on axis 5 sixty," that doesn't give any information to a court. It's the same if I give to the court only the conclusion that this person is suffering from an anti-social personality disorder. I need to explain what an anti-social personality disorder is, and I need to explain why this person is suffering from that disorder. And then afterwards, I need to evaluate what are the possible consequences of suffering from that disorder. So it's the same with axis 5, and I think usually it is not relevant for the information the court needs. It is relevant if I am a family doctor or I'm a psychiatrist in a community mental health centre and I have to refer the patient for admission to a mental hospital. Then it may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So it's either irrelevant or Judges wouldn't understand it or it's just not useful to them; is that what you're saying, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm saying to you that if I give the information to the court that somebody is scoring 60 at axis 5, that doesn't say anything at all for the court, and I think that is right. They are not psychiatrists. So I need to describe how somebody was functioning in a certain period. I describe it in an evaluation, of course, I always do. I repeat what I wrote down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, when you arrived at your conclusion, there was another psychiatrist, a Dr. Lagazzi from Italy. Did you read his report at any time in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you rely on his report in coming to the conclusions you discussed today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which report do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, he wrote two of them, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but which of my reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, let's start off with which of your reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one, he wasn't in the picture, so when I had the first evaluation to do, he wasn't there -- he was but not in this issue. The second evaluation, he was appointed too, so we had two conversations with each other. And in those conversations, we just talked with each other. We combined our experiences, our clinical experience, and how we were thinking about it. Our conclusion was that we had, roughly speaking, the same opinion. That was the second one. The third one, we had a complete meeting with each other and with the third psychiatrist, and Mrs. de Sampayo had asked us to do so and we did so. It was a very fruitful meeting from a professional point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In arriving at the opinions that you gave here today, did you rely on any of the factual statements that are in Dr. Lagazzi's reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The facts related to Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clinical facts or facts in the sense of life events?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Facts in the sense of life events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't rely upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You didn't rely upon those. Okay, that's fair enough. You say that Mr. Landzo is being treated twice a week by a Dutch psychologist. Have you reviewed that psychologist's notes or reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't have been allowed to do so. I telephoned him, and he said to me he didn't want to give me detailed information, but he confirmed to me too that he talked with Mr. Landzo twice a week. I said to him that I was deeply impressed by the result, and he said, "Thank you." So you can say that he understood what I was meaning, and I think I understood how he was working. But it would be impossible, because he wants to keep himself completely free of the criminal law procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can understand that. Doctor, I'll be right up front with you. I retained a psychiatrist to interview my client, and he is what is called a cross-cultural psychiatrist. He is an expert and teaches cross-cultural psychiatry at McGill University in Montreal, Canada. Tell the Judges what cross-cultural psychiatry is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm working in Holland, and I can assure you that doing this work for quite a number of years, I got very much used to the example of the Northern African countries, because I have to evaluate many persons who partly belong to that culture. It's the same with persons who have their origins in the Dutch Antilles or in Suriname, and now even I have to evaluate persons who are refugees from African or Eastern European countries. I think as a forensic psychiatrist, if you do this work intensively, then you need to develop a cross-cultural way of thinking. The only thing you say is that with your interpretations, you need always to keep in mind what is the cultural background of that person, even if I evaluated a Dutchman who grew up in a sub-cultural background which is completely different than mine. So in psychiatry, you need always to have the ability to think in cross-cultural terms and to be careful with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The reason for that, Doctor, would be that what might be perfectly sane for me to do as an American may be insane for someone in - pick a country - Burma. On the other hand, what may be a perfectly sane and reasonable way of behaving in Burma may be perceived to be way outside of the norms in the United States; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now you will get an answer you don't like, yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I like all the answers, as long as they are truthful, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that's true. Let's say especially the personality disorders, they have a cultural aspect. For example, I read an article from a Dutch psychiatrist who interviewed 45 psychiatrists in India, and they said, "A dependent personality is a normal personality in our country and an avoiding personality, it belongs to our culture to be always avoiding." So that's true, then you have a cultural feeling. For example, medical symptoms, they have dual qualities. Schizophrenia, it has had lots of research from the World Health Organisation, and schizophrenia is a disease which is everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Doctor, may I say something? It has something to do with the values in each society, in each culture. For example, let's take attitudes towards sex. It may be perfectly normal in Holland, but it may be revolting in Pakistan. And sometimes what is important to you gives you this sense. So maybe the attitudes are different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you. Therefore, you always need to be careful with your interpretations, and you need to cross-examine your own cultural standards that you don't -- because if you make your own cultural standard to the proof of being sane or insane, then you are wrong. I think you understood me very well. Thank you. I think that it depends, it depends. For example, this adjustment disorder, I think you can work with it in every country, but you need always to be careful. Is this a medical symptom for that person? That's an international standard, because the international standard for a medical symptom is that you are suffering from it. Therefore, my answer is yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me go ahead to a slightly different topic. You testified that basically you're relying on reaching your opinions on what Esad Landzo told you. The long and the sort of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, partly, because I have the ability to make my own clinical judgments. So I interview, I listen to the facts, I listen to his life history, and I observe him, yes? I'm trained for that. Then I make a measure of all these things, so that's one part of an evaluation. Second, I listen to his information about his life history, but I haven't joined his life, yes? So I must rely upon it. He told me about what he did in that Celebici camp, and then I always repeat again, I'm not in a position to tell whether it is true or not. That's the job of the lawyers. So it's very easy. I only described what he told me, because then you can argue, you can investigate, as to whether it's true or not. I only say, "If that is true on the side of the facts, then this is my interpretation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For instance, when you met with him the second time in November of 1996 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- there was -- let me back off a second. You've described him as a dependent personality. Does that mean if there is a strong authority figure, he would become dependent on that authority figure and do what that authority figure told him to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I saw him, he was in a rather bad mental condition. I will never forget -- I was something like an authority. We talked quietly. It was a quiet atmosphere. Maybe it was the first time he could talk with somebody. First he had done with the psychiatrist from Bosnia, but I'm not quite sure that was completely in a quiet atmosphere. With me, I explained to him a few things and he talked with me. I will never forget when I went away, he was asking, "When do you come back?" So he changed. Then afterwards, I'm sure his Defence counsel, she's filling him. The psychotherapist, he is filling his emptiness. Now he is doing what his psychotherapist is telling him, but he is going, he is going, that I noticed. But nevertheless, all we know is he has other persons who gave him other messages, but still he is a dependent person. I could observe it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, the second time you visited him which was, what, about three weeks after the first time, he exhibited quite a bit of more aberrant behaviour, for lack of a better term, didn't he? Let me give you an example. What is a dissociative phenomena, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was described in my secondary report. I was telephoned by Mrs. De Sampayo. She told me that he had shown some kind of behaviour during some of the sessions at that time for this Tribunal. So I heard those things, and Mr. Landzo told me a bit about it, but I described in my report that I didn't see them in the hours I was talking with him. And what a dissociative state is, I described it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. Doctor, does the DSM-IV use the phrase "malingering"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Malingering"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to borrow my copy of it, you can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The book I have is Dutch. I think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What is malingering, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is that you are playing a disease. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you know that you are doing so. That's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it's to fool other folks, right, to fool other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you know why you do it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, DMS-IV warns practitioners in a medical/legal context that there's a strong possibility of malingering, doesn't it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you are working as a forensic psychiatrist, you get everyday training in this field. I can assure you, if you work in a prison, every prisoner will say to you, "I need to see my wife, and you are a psychiatrist, so you understand how important it is for me. Please take care that I see my wife tomorrow at home." So those things, I'm used to it. But I always say it is not so difficult to discover whether somebody is malingering or not. There is something else if they are manipulating. Do you see the difference? Malingering, how can I defend myself against it, because I don't talk quite often for an hour with somebody. Then I would have a danger. I talk hours and hours. Usually in many cases, many times. Then I get a real clinical judgment. Usually, the person I'm talking with doesn't know what is relevant for me or not. Sometimes I ask somebody who is trying to malinger. It is so easy to be detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doesn't the American Psychiatric Association in DSM-IV warn practitioners that they should try to get information from third sources, more reliable sources? I believe the phrase they use is "collateral sources"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You always like them if you can get them, but you need to work with what you can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall on direct examination, I'm not trying to put words in your mouth, I'm relying on my own notes, okay? If my notes are wrong, what I am about to say is wrong. I just want to say that. The first time you met or the first couple of times you met with Mr. Landzo, I guess until a week ago Sunday, he denied any involvement in any bad acts at Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you've read his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have read the oral statement he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You've read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I described it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. In that, he denies any involvement with any bad acts, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said on direct that his Bosnian attorney had advised him to deny it; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He talked to me last Sunday, and I must say that at the end of 1996, Mr. Lagazzi telephoned me. We said to each other that we had the impression that something like that may occur, but it was not our task to talk about it officially. Why do I tell this to you, to the court? I was not surprised when Mr. Landzo told me, and I am not even more surprised because it proves again how dependent he is. Because I remember when I told the court earlier in this testimony, that I felt he was very much willing to talk completely with me. I could feel it, but I had to respect his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. That's fair enough. You think that the reason he lied was because he was dependent on his Bosnian attorney and his Bosnian attorney told him to lie? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the term "lying." He is not saying he lied. He said he respected his position of denying the allegations at the time. That is not considered a lie by any stretch of the imagination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The advice his counsel gave him, is that not privileged?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that when the advice that counsel has given is revealed to a third party that that is not a waiver of the privilege. In any case, I'm not asking what advice counsel gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Deny the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Deny the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Any privilege was probably waived by telling a third party about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not the one giving that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In any case, it was your opinion, based on your meeting with Mr. Landzo a week ago Sunday, that the reason he made these denials was because of a dependent personality and things told to him by his then lawyer? I think that's what you said on direct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and because the Defence lawyer of Mr. Landzo asked me questions about probability, and that I refer to again. So it was, for me, quite probable, but not more than that, because I never can say more than that, that he did so because his Defence lawyer at that time said to him so, because that is completely -- you can completely explain that thing from his person. I think in his psychotherapy, I'm quite sure that the psychotherapist works with the whole matter, listening very much, being interested, being empathic. Mr. Landzo said in that climate, he took the position to change his position, what he called to tell the truth, to tell what happened, to tell what happened. Those were his words. I don't know, and it's impossible to get that information, but I think that his therapist has given him some kind of message that the only way to survive all these experiences is to come out with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the psychotherapist is not a dominant person, because a psychotherapist never -- is never allowed to be so, but he's very influential again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, a psychotherapist can be the most important person in your life. Maybe he shouldn't be but can be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a question, I think, for another --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Another time, another place. You said that Mr. Landzo currently suffers from post-traumatic stress syndrome, PTSD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was not at the time of May 1992, but I think that started maybe -- it started in the Bosnian prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To develop the symptoms of a post-traumatic stress disorder. Anyhow, when I observed him for the first time, they weren't really the symptoms which belonged to a person with post-traumatic stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is counsel's book. Do you need it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I may need that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'll give it back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I may need it now. I can lend it to you over lunch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will give it to you immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, any diagnosis of PTSD that may be made now is irrelevant to anything that occurred in the summer of 1992; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion, because I need to warn that it's a fluent development from an adjustment disorder to a post-traumatic stress disorder. I started to say earlier that a human being is complicated, we all know. For example, he had the war circumstances. He had some traumatic events, but maybe he would have got adjusted to it later, after the war. But immediately from the war conditions, he entered into the prison, and that is absolutely not the right place to get adjusted to a traumatic experience. And even you may say that he had a new traumatic experience, because being a prisoner, you are in a situation of others have the power and you don't have any power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You also said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you referring to your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite frankly, I'm a bit nervous about what I am going to hear later from other witnesses; secondly, although this Trial Chamber has said that nothing that comes out of the mouths of these physicians will be used against my client, somebody else may look at this record in the future, and if they rely upon it, for instance, in assessing the legal sufficiency of evidence, I don't want it to be said by some other judges at some other time and some other place that I had a chance to cross-examine somebody and didn't do it. The court understands what I'm doing? Secondly, I don't know -- again, I don't know what other witnesses might say, and I think I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If other witnesses say something against your client, you can cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether anything affects your client, you can ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm not stopping you. I was just thinking of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you will allow me to give a quick reaction, because to demonstrate to you what I mean, if you would give me somebody else the order to evaluate your client, I could do it, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I think only in a sense of interactions and not in the sense of guilt. So if I should get that order, I should do it completely free and independently again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it's not my position to be against somebody or defending somebody. I'm just doing clinical work, but that's a quick reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm the lawyer and I defend people and you're the physician and psychiatrist and you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's very important to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that. You're a scientist. In fact, you're the second scientist in three days to sit in that chair. Last week I brought my scientist on, and I understand where you're coming from and you're doing the best you can. Without going into any great details, you said that when he joined the army, he wasn't a mature person and he didn't have any reserves of personality and became very dependent on other people. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need to say how it was. The reality is that he was in war circumstances. We can assume that he was. I can judge that he has a dependent personality, so then you can make some conclusions. Then second, if it is proven that he was under the influence of another person in that special situation, then my interpretation is that that influence is clinically relevant, you see? And I don't see a contrary thing. I'm not in a position to say he was under the influence of another person. No, he said he was, and this is my interpretation. And then afterwards, you need to prove whether that was true or not, whether he was in that position. Do you understand? That's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. That's fair enough, Doctor. Doctor, you talked about his dependency on his brother and his brother's friends prior to the war. Do you know anything about what he and his brother and his brother's friends did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what he told me was that they drank quite a lot. They bought drinks, alcoholic beverages in the shops, and they put all the money they had together and then drank it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be -- in my country, for young people to do that, we're talking about cross-cultural, might be very reasonable. And in Pakistan, that might be very unreasonable for young people to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You get lashes for drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I'm glad that I don't live in Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Tom would look very black and blue at this point, I promise you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, the situation he described was not something I had any idea to do. That situation has proven that he was suffering from something, for me, the important thing was that he couldn't make his own friends. So he was in a circle, he got an easy entrance by means of his brother, and in the circle of boys, he was about 17 and they were 19 to 20. That had some relevance for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm a little worried about your interpretation of dependency. Now, if you consider the situation of the priest, the priest in religion, the priest of any church, who takes out of obedience, and the feelings of their military and their superiors, who must obey their superiors directions? Now, in what category do you put such situations if you regard dependency as one of the conditions for determining the person's vulnerability to set in traits which you have indicated. These are situations that are accepted. So a priest must be, a soldier must be, so how then do you regard this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your question because that gives me the possibility to explain exactly what I mean. I think you may have a priest who gives up his own personality, maybe because he has never had a personality. And then being a priest is some kind of a solution for that person, and you have other persons who choose to become a priest, they have their own reasons for it, and as a priest, they remain -- they keep their own personality. They keep the ability to think, they keep the ability to make decisions within a certain framework. The same you can say about soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But they still must obey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. But there's a difference between knowing that you are obeying because the situation asks you to obey, or obeying with closed eyes because you can't do anything else than obey. And you can't do anything else than obeying with closed eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My fear is that this does not necessarily explain the person's personality, because if the person is in such a situation in which he must obey or suffer the penalty for disobedience, you cannot bring that within the purview of somebody who has, what you call, a personality trait, which makes him subjected to such situations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that -- I remember when I was working in the army, that was in the beginning after I had finished my medical studies and I started psychiatric residency, we had to evaluate persons who wanted to become military soldiers. One of the instructions we got is take care that this is a person with which can be independent, even in a military police section, they prefer people who can obey, but who can be independent too. And if they had traits of great dependency, we got instruction, "We don't want him." So making a diagnosis is not something like looking five seconds and then I have my diagnosis. It's like a puzzle, do you understand, a puzzle, little things, you put them together, and then you get all these little things together and then you recognise something. I don't say Mr. Landzo has a dependent personality trait to such a clinical extent that they make him vulnerable because he said to me he was obeying in that camp. No, because I saw it. I saw the repetition, yes, his lawyer, his brother, his lawyer, a Defence lawyer, his new Defence lawyer, his psychotherapist. So at the moment his mental condition is good because his inner life is filled at the moment, you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to relate that to the general situation of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the situation you described, they have nothing to do with the personality disorder. This is a situation, and if you choose for that situation, you know the consequences, but you can still use your brain. But if have you a personality disorder, you can't use any more of your brain, and then it can be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just didn't want to interrupt you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You say you worked in the army and this is the first I heard about that. Militaries all over the world recruit young folks, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, if I told that you the British army typically recruits people at age 16, you wouldn't disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you tell me, I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I saw that on BBC last week so that's where that came from. I can tell you that the United States military recruits people at age 17, some of whom have not completed high school. And I don't know what age the Dutch army starts recruiting people, but just because they are young and immature doesn't mean that they are just going to look at a first sergeant that's been in the military for 15 years and just blindly do whatever that man says, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the reality is that at the moment, because until two years ago, we had a professional army, partly, and every boy from about 18 to 19 had to enter the army for one half year, or if you became an officer for 21 months, unless you were not capable, you didn't have enough abilities to do your military service. But at the moment, we have a professional army, so a boy of 17 can think, "I want to enter that army," but our army doesn't say "Oh, yes, you want to join us. Please be welcome. You will be examined too." And I think -- and then afterwards, you enter the army, and if you can't sustain the situation, then you are thrown out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it is not a matter of only of mature persons, no. They are persons who are young. They need to be developed. But in a modern way of thinking, an army is professional. Being in the army is doing your job, and you get trained to do that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. By the way, Mr. Landzo is not mentally retarded or anything like that? He is a bright guy, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you mean with the word mentally retarded --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He is not dumb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we call, intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, he is above average intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. The first psychologist tried to do testing, I remember, and if I see how he is talking English now, then he is absolutely from at least of average intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm here to tell that you his English is much better than my Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that doesn't mean anything at all, and I'll plead guilty to speaking about four words in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So we're not talking about a person of less than average intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, he's probably a little above average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Probably felt a little frustrated when he couldn't go to art school. Doctor, in fact, I think I may have mentioned it, have you ever heard of a diagnosis in DMS-IV called anti-social personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me whether I have heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And DSM-IV -- by the way -- well, let me back off. DSM-IV points out that deceit and manipulation are central features of anti-social personality disorder, and then it goes on to say: "It might be especially helpful to integrate information acquired from other systematic clinical assessment with information collected from collateral sources when reaching that diagnosis." Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, people with anti-social personality disorder are pretty good liars, aren't they, as a group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You say as a group. That depends. That depends. You see, because I see about 30 to 40 inmates a week. I talk with them, and the majority of them, you could say they have an anti-social personality disorder, so I'm very used to the disorder. I know some of them lie, some of them don't lie. That depends upon the situation. Sometimes they even -- even me they trust and they don't lie, but it's not easy for them to trust somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What are the symptoms of anti-social personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would it be helpful if I lent you DSM-IV and you could have it right in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but one of the symptoms is that you have criminal behaviour and that otherwise you set fire when you're a school boy, that you started to steal, taking things and not paying for it, even as a school boy, that you are manipulating, that you are lying, that you are not reliable, that you are sexually very promiscuous; do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. You also have things pop up like, for instance -- strike that. People with anti-social personality disorder, they are not crazy? They are not nuts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Crazy is not a clinical word. If you mean by crazy, psychotic, then I can follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Psychotic is people that are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is another kind of disease in a personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Psychotic is people who see snakes coming out of the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a sign of a psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You haven't seen that in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Anti-social personality disorder used to be known by some other names, didn't it? How about sociopath or sociopathy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That word hasn't had a long history like the word psychopath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I notice that you said that someone who loves dogs, it doesn't mean that he has a personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I love dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought I would pass along to you that there's a saying in Washington, D.C. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are rehashing his evidence. If you have finished what you have to ask, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am --. Let me look at my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know, Doctor, if Mr. Landzo claimed to have committed violent acts outside of the abnormal violent acts? Now, if someone, for instance, is in the infantry in the army, they are going to engage in violent acts if they are in combat. But setting that aside, do you know if Mr. Landzo has claimed of committed any inappropriate violent acts outside of any reference to what's in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the war situation or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I say, setting aside what one would expect from a soldier in combat, I would expect that a soldier in combat, if he saw the enemy coming at him, he would shoot him, and that's a violent act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On the other hand, there was an incident involving my army during the Vietnam war called My Lai where an officer in the United States army gunned down 120 people. I would call that inappropriate violence. Do you know -- but that would be involved in wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then, on the other hand, I have had clients who have engaged in inappropriate violence by shooting convenience store clerks during robberies. So when I say "inappropriate violence" that's a pretty wide scope. This, I guess, just calls for a yes or no. Aside from the allegations in the indictment, do you know whether Mr. Landzo has claimed to have engaged in any, what I would call, inappropriate violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me why he got his eight-year sentence and he went and he had to stay in the prison two years. He told me the reason for it, but he said to me that he was alleged to have committed a murder and this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But he told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is the only inappropriate violence you know about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only story I heard about. I said a story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and after lunch I may have no further questions, but I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will reassemble at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before my colleague continues, may I inform you that my colleague, Professor O'Sullivan has other obligations this afternoon and he will be absent from the courtroom, with your permission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you still continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For about five minutes, Your Honour, will be about all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, over the lunch hour -- by the way, I hope you had a good lunch. Over the lunch hour, did you discuss your testimony with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Doctor, you say that you are familiar with the findings of Dr. Lagazzi or at least you're familiar with what he found and his diagnosis of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the cases, finding it back in my second and third report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you're familiar with it today, where you're sitting right now, you're familiar with what he had in his report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just two reports, I have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You don't have the third report that I was just handed about two minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to ask you something based on the facts that he outlines in those reports. They are fairly straightforward questions. Doctor, if you have someone who gets drunks with a bunch of his buddies, a bunch of his co-fighters, and takes a woman and suspends her from the top of a tall building by holding her by her heels because she refused to go with him, and when they hear her crying, they pull her up to safety. Would that be more consistent with anti-personality disorder or would that be more consistent with this kind of disorder that you were talking about or this dependency disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This question can't be answered with the information you gave me. I should need much more information by means of an assessment, with the need of the assessment. I could only formulate a hypothesis from the information you gave me. It is clearly not enough for any clinical judgment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about this, Doctor: How about a person who is promised a house to move into, but when he shows up at the door drunk, he finds four girls there inside this house, so he becomes angry and tosses in a hand grenade and fires a burst of machine gun fire, injures one of the girls --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object that this line of questioning with hypotheticals that has nothing to do with this case is totally irrelevant and out of line with this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Someone who is drunk, he can behave anyhow. You don't have to bother with that. Any other relevant questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether, after the period he was in Celebici, whether or not Mr. Landzo was assigned to any other units in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that also part of his assessment of his mental health?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know what he did while he was assigned to those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me before Celebici --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm asking about after Celebici, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember what he told me what he did before Celebici, that I remember. And then after Celebici, shortly afterwards, he went to that other camp. Then he told me he was in the army, but then he was 56 days in gaol without any -- he didn't know why. And then afterwards, I believe shortly afterwards, he came into gaol again, and that was the case which ended in the eight-year sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the rest of his active service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me a tiny little bit, but I thought it was a very short period, as far as I remember, no substantial information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, given the information you have, including the reports you've examined and the other doctors you've talked to, would it be fair to say that a diagnosis of personality disorder mixed with predominant features including characteristics of both schizoid, anti-social personality disorder; would you say that's a fair diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could a competent physician make that diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything is possible. I don't know how competent that colleague would be, but if you know Mr. Landzo very well, you need to have really done a thorough evaluation, assessment. Then you should understand that the key problems concerning the personality structure of Mr. Landzo is different with the key problems of somebody suffering from anti-social personality disorder. So that's more a psychodynamic point of view. And then afterwards, if you reduce yourself to the rather easy descriptive way of describing in the DSM-IV, even then he doesn't show the characteristics of the anti-social personality disorder as described in DSM-IV, and I mentioned them already. He didn't commit crimes before anyhow. As far as I know, he was not sexually promiscuous. He didn't set fire. He didn't steal things. But more important, if you have met him, if you really start to know him, then you understand he has other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So someone that would make that diagnosis would just be wrong, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecution, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May I be a little helpful. The Defence of the accused is one of diminished responsibility, and I suppose that is what the experts are required to testify to. So you might as well direct your questions to that aspect of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I intend to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. van Leeuwen. My name is Jim Cowles. I represent the Prosecutor in this matter. Dr. van Leeuwen, you have testified that you do not diagnose any post-traumatic stress disorder in Mr. Landzo in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And the specific personality disorder that you do diagnose of Mr. Landzo in 1992 is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told, it's a mixed personality disorder with borderline schizoid and dependent traits.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And you have discussed or used previous reports rendered by Dr. Lagazzi in this matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't use the reports, but I remember when we had that meeting at the beginning of January, January 1997, and we discussed the whole evening with each other, with Mr. Lagazzi, then it was Loga, then we discovered that we had the same clinical opinion about the nature of his personality disorder and the nature of his vulnerabilities. So I didn't build up my clinical judgment about his personality by reading. I had my opinion, and afterwards, I read those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Then you are aware that Dr. Lagazzi did, indeed, diagnose Mr. Landzo with post-traumatic stress disorder in his report of November 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You found post-traumatic stress disorder --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: At the time of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And that had to do with the questions I had to answer in the first and second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that Dr. Lagazzi did not diagnose post-traumatic stress disorder in Mr. Landzo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. It is your testimony that Mr. Landzo does not have a lack of mental responsibility; in other words, insanity; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You're saying he has a diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has -- for reasons I told and I explained --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. This has been asked and answered and explained over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is cross-examination by him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. So he had, from a clinical point of view, he had a diminished capacity to exercise his own free will, and I mean "will" as a psychological function, mental function. And then if that is your conclusion and your conclusion is that the capacity is diminished because of a lack of mental capacity or together with a mental disorder, then the consequences in forensic psychiatric field that you are given advice for a diminished criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Doctor, in your report dated 13 January 1997, which was your last of the three reports you rendered, you indicate that: "It remains unclear whether or not the subject meets the criteria of a personality disorder." On page 15 of that report, in the paragraph beginning with "On the basis of ..."; you don't see that? I'm looking at the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The second paragraph, the second paragraph of page 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on page 16, that's my original report, I said: "It is more sensible and safer to say he has a personality with schizoid traits." If you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: No, I was referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I went on with "That has to do with personality disorder." I think then it is better to talk about vulnerabilities. That is what I explained to the court. If you talk about a personality disorder, you talk about vulnerability for circumstances. Everyone is vulnerable, but somebody who has a personality disorder is more than the average person in that culture for average circumstances or extreme circumstances vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: He may be vulnerable, Doctor, but what do you mean in this report -- on my copy of the report, I believe it's the copy that's been entered in the record, on page 15, that the subject -- "It is unclear whether or not the subject meets the criteria of a personality disorder." I don't know if you have the same copy that's been filed with the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's the report dated the 10th of January. If you look at page 15, the second paragraph which is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you give me your translation, because then I can find it back in mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: The second paragraph at the top third of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you prefer the Dutch version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be on page 17. I've got it. In my copy, page 17 is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Do you have it now in your copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't find it because I'm missing my page but it's covered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean in the Dutch version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the Dutch original. Yes, the reason was that I sat at that moment at this very dangerous to conclude to a personality disorder because we don't know how he would have developed himself without that war; do you understand? So I said for any other vulnerabilities, I could recognise at the moment, but from a viewpoint of the investigation assessment, I had the problem that he was really in a depressed mood. He was not to be interviewed as I could do now, a week ago first, so you had the mask of disease, mental disease, at that time. But especially in the field of interpretation, you had the problem that from the early adulthood, he was under extreme circumstances. So what he -- it ranges to include the interpretation, that includes to a personality disorder. I feel myself no better informed with the -- because now he is in a good mental condition. You can talk with him freely, and you can witness the developments he has made the last one-half year, and then you see it repeats and repeats. And then he could give me a bit more information. I didn't change my mind, but at that moment, I needed to be more careful with my interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned a good deal about vulnerabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That you found in Mr. Landzo. Where, exactly, in the DSM-IV does it refer to vulnerabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Under any description or diagnostic criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DSM IV is just description, description, description, and if I talk about vulnerability, then I'm more thinking in a more psychodynamic way which reveals more of the reality of a human being. If I'm revealing to the court, I need to try anyhow, to reveal the reality about that person, and a person is more than a reduction of symptoms. That's the weakness of the DSM-IV, but the strength of the DSM-IV is that we can communicate with each other, but it doesn't reveal the truth of a human being. And vulnerability, that describes more the psychodynamic aspects of a human being. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Where does that term or how does that diagnosis fit under any criteria under any personality disorder in the DSM-IV? Can you point to a section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just said that DSM-IV (indiscernible). DSM-IV is nothing more than a way of describing categories, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Which is internationally recognised as a criteria to describe personality disorders; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the general criteria and a special -- the inflexible and the maledictive traits, which is very important, and which causes significant distress or impairment of social or occupational or other important areas of functioning. Those are general characteristics, and that you can translate in the term of vulnerabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back for just a second to Dr. Lagazzi's report rendered at the same time you rendered your reports, his report states that at the time the incident happened, the accused was influenced by psychopathological disorder --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object right now. He said he didn't rely on Dr. Lagazzi's report to form his opinion. Dr. Lagazzi will be here to testify about his report and that would be the best source for questioning about Dr. Lagazzi's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He told you that he made his own independent examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: When you indicate, Doctor, that he is vulnerable then, does that fit with your description of him that he can be led, that he is susceptible to be being told what to do and he will obey orders, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I answered to the court when I got that question. Obeying has nothing to do with disease or a lack of mental capacity on its own. It is the way you are obeying and the intensity. And then you get again, the general characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You didn't find any mental disease or mental defect in Mr. Landzo, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: A disease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look at this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You're saying that he has a disease but you're not saying that he has a lack of responsibility at all; correct? He's not insane at the time of 1992, was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's been asked and answered. He's not talking about insanity at all and he keeps referring to insanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the doctor has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please conclude with your questioning. The doctor is here to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Doctor, your findings of Mr. Landzo indicate that he was fully aware of his actions in 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And your findings indicate that he also understood the wrongfulness of any deeds and he was aware of his actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I think we were talking about killing all the people. I think everyone in the world knows that that is not allowed, as an act.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So he was aware of moral consequences in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on that basic level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a report rendered in 1994 when Mr. Landzo was examined by other doctors in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: One doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You're familiar with that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you aware of his conclusion that, and I quote "During the commission of the crime, the subject was able to comprehend the significance of his act and his ability to control his acts was reduced but not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting. The Prosecutor is testifying from a document that is not in evidence. If he wants to ask Dr. van Leeuwen about what he knows about the report, that's different. But the Prosecutor is testifying right now and offering evidence before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I was asking the doctor is he is familiar with this doctor's report, and Dr. van Leeuwen indicated he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him whether he knows about the report and the conclusions of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the conclusions of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I must warn you and everyone, because that was a report about another act than we are talking about here. Criminal responsibility is not a personality trait. Criminal responsibility represents somebody's mental state at the moment of a certain act or certain acts, and a combination of that mental state and the interference of that mental state and those acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Doctor, strictly speaking, this is what you are here to tell the Trial Chamber. What counsel for the accused has asked you to come and say is that "Our client is suffering under a diminished responsibility for his acts." And that is what you are here to testify about. It refers to criminal responsibility and that it is less than what is expected of somebody who lacks criminal responsibility for committing an act. This is what you are here to testify about after examining him. How did you come to the conclusions that his capacity to commit those acts have been diminished by virtue of his mental state? This is what you are expected to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's what counsel is leading you to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I just want to offer an objection right now. The Prosecutor is going into a set of facts that have nothing to do with Mr. Landzo's mental capacity in 1992 in Celebici, and it's irrelevant to these proceedings, and the court has ruled that that was irrelevant to these proceedings before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He hasn't stated any set of facts. All he pointed out was the conclusion of another doctor, which this expert knows very well, and whether he agreed with it. That was the question he asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to clear up, this doctor that the Prosecutor is referring to examined Mr. Landzo in regard to another set of circumstances that have nothing to do with Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: About his criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With some other -- not having to do with Celebici, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a report which was tendered to the Trial Chamber. It was not a report which was done outside this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was done in Zenica prison in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know about that. The 1994 situation was not what was tendered to us here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought that incident took place in Celebici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, the report of this doctor was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the incident which the doctor referred to in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, Your Honour, the allegation was that it occurred in Celebici in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I intend to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, go on to something else. Confine yourself to reports which have been tendered to the Trial Chamber in respect of which you rely opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like to respond to Judge Jan's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it has anything to do with the question he's asking. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, the diminished responsibility issue; you are unable to give a percentage or a level of diminished responsibility, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a percentage, because a human being, and especially the mental state of a human being, you can't reduce it to the measure of 25, 51 per cent or something like it. I'm used to a system where we have on the one side, you have criminal responsibility, and the other side you have criminal not responsibility, and then you have a whole field between. And then I always use as a metaphor, if somebody has a fever, you can have a fever of 38 degrees, do you understand 38 degrees celsius? Then you can still make a choice whether you stay in bed or not. If you like your work, you go out of bed and continue your work. If you have 40 degrees, you can still go to work but it is not easy to go to work, and that is an interference I'm trained for as a clinician. So I say somebody has some kind of a mental disorder at that particular time, and you may expect that that has such a lot of influence on his capacities, that he was between 0 and 100, between the two extremes, he was somewhere in between. And that you express as diminished, somewhere between. But in Holland, we use a sliding scale with the slightly diminished or strongly diminished or diminished.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: No system that you're aware of does diminished responsibility ever exculpate a person from criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's a question of law. How would he know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You said no system of law. There are hundreds of systems of law. How can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Doctor, the incident that Mr. Landzo did admit to you, that he beat a man to death; did he say that he did it under orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me strictly that that was the only time he did so without an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Without an order. So how is that related to diminished responsibility as a result of a personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The case of the Defence is he didn't have the free will. Under the circumstances there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So he couldn't help himself; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say he couldn't at all. I think that experience -- you see, if you find, I just tell you what he told me and I repeat what I said before. He said to me that he saw, I believe, 8 people. They were killed in a cruel way. He discovered one man who he loved very much. That is a very stressful event for everyone, but he was in a state, in a condition, that he couldn't settle down with it partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. If he is unable to act out of his free will, and so he was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Partly, all right. As a result of this personality disorder, was this personality disorder -- did this come about in his earlier life, during the course of his earlier life, correct, not by a single incident that occurred that may have occurred during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personality -- therefore, I was careful at that time when I made my third report, because a personality disorder is growing during -- from the birth, and nowadays, we say the genetic factors are important too, but it is growing. You see the presigns. The presigns are the first signs you see in the early development, and then adulthood starts, and then you see the personality disorder expresses the way of life of that person, and then you can recognise the personality disorder. So it is not -- it had nothing to do with an event, but I didn't say, and I must repeat what I show you here and what I said before, a personality disorder in itself never explains a criminal act. It is always an interaction of the personality disorder and specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Such as free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that interaction produces some of these disorders, and that disorder influences the capacity to exercise your will.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree that most criminals could be diagnosed as having some kind of personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very strict with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very strict with it. I always say, "If you are not strict with the general criteria, then every criminal is suffering from an anti-social personality disorder. It absolutely doesn't work. I don't want to work in that way of thinking. I'm very careful, because I think "disorder" is a vague word and you need to use it very carefully and especially forensic psychiatry. If you do it in clinical practice, okay, but in forensic psychiatry, that's the whole basis for your advice about criminal responsibility, so you need to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And if you find or you do diagnose a personality disorder in a criminal who is charged with committing a criminal act, do you always find diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no, it depends from case to case.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always want to assess the special case, the special person, the special dossier, the special accusations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And Mr. Landzo's case, the special things in his life, were that he was a frustrated art student, he liked stray dogs, he didn't have many friends, he was easily led, he was vulnerable to be influenced. Couldn't that describe an awful lot of people, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't say an awful lot, but, of course. But then you get the degree of severeness too. If you, in your younger years, you live in the woods, you love to be in the woods together with a dog, sleeping in a hole with a dog, that's quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that Mr. Landzo, you know that Mr. Landzo abused drugs and alcohol during 1992, during the time of the war experiences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't the testimony that he abused drugs. The testimony was that he used them to sleep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Use the proper evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Landzo used alcohol and drugs during the time in question in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked with him about it and he didn't deny that he was drinking, and he liked to drink, and he combined it with Akineton because he discovered that alcohol had more influence, but I put the question very directly to him, and he answered me that he never had drinks when he was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Very well then. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony that because of his condition that no matter what type of crime he may have committed or if the facts showed that he, indeed, committed a crime, that he would have some degree of diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time that I was producing my third report, I had to do it in that way. Not everyone -- some people, some forensics are going to say if somebody is denying, I don't see anything at all. To my opinion, I can assure you in Holland, I'm used to working here, many colleagues share my opinion, and that it differs from case to case. Sometimes you must say that I can only -- I have only the possibility to describe the kind of disturbance, of disorder, at the time of the act when I can talk with somebody about the criminal act. Yes? Other cases, you say, I see such a huge amount of disorder, and I read what act could have been, then I can combine it, but not very precisely, just roughly, and that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: In your examination with Mr. Landzo, you had no -- did you have any information about facts that he is alleged to have committed during the time, during the summer of 1992 in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got, what do you call that, confinement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If I may assist. He had a copy of the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The indictment I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That's just the formal charge, you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a lot of detail. I don't remember. It was very detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Have you had the benefit of any other descriptions or any other information given to you about acts that Mr. Landzo is alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got recently from the Defence counsel, I got a map, and I started to read it, but I'm a psychiatrist, so if I read those things, I'm not interested in -- that he -- did he do this or did he do that, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only want to have an idea. What kind of acts are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a few. Backing up just a second, when you said you're examining someone and you decide or you think there's going to be diminished responsibility, but the individual denies having done anything to begin with, you can't find out what diminished responsibility exists, right, because he denies the facts that underlie the act that gave rise to alleged diminished responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, again, I repeat my metaphor of fever. Sometimes you have such a lot of information, you get a clear description of acts, criminal acts, which are alleged on the one side, and on the other side I get a clear picture of the nature and the severeness of the mental disorder.
