Then I can say roughly -- and there I did, there is not any indication for any criminal responsibility, but on the other side, I presume there's some kind of diminished responsibility, but I can't make it precise for you because I can't ask the questions: Why did you do that? What did you feel in that moment? Those questions I could have asked to Mr. Landzo last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Would it be helpful to you then, as a doctor, giving this information to the court to have had information or to have information about facts he is alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because -- only to start my conversation. I can say to somebody, you are alleged that you have done that. If he says no, I haven't done it, then it's finished. If he says yes, that I have done, then I go on. So it is not for my -- sometimes it is useful just to make your starting hypothesis, but then you need your further investigation, and I have my own ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: If the facts of the case -- let's put it this way: If the testimony has been rendered in this court in the past, concerning Mr. Landzo, specifically, about physical things he did and acts he took; wouldn't that be helpful to you as a forensic psychiatrist to determine if the man was acting under free will completely, 100 per cent, or less than something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The accuracy of those facts is yet to be determined.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was going to say I object because those are allegations by the Prosecution which have not been proven and they are not relevant to this determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: They are facts in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are accuracy to be determined yet by this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What the doctor had done himself is an examination of the accused person.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Then may I pose a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not on what he hasn't examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May I pose the facts -- may I pose a testimony that has been adduced in court by witnesses in the form of a hypothetical situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That doesn't concern him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is hypothetical. It will be of no use to. Too hypothetical for us to take into account. The accuracy of those facts is yet to be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has examined the accused. We want to have the experience of his examination, not things which would come later.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on from that then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, you know nothing about the allegations or the facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And that is it, Dr. van Leeuwen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that characterisation. He has read statements, much more information than just the indictment. I believe the Prosecutor has misstated what he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I didn't misstate anything, Your Honour. I'm asking the Doctor what information he has about the facts of the case and he has told me only the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the facts of the case are what the indictment alleges. They are no facts of this until the court determines its verdict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have heard the argument about this. The doctor was concerned with examining the accused person and that he has done, and we are limited to his experience from his examination, and not more. He has told us what he has done and it is under that that you should ask him questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say that that indictment was very clear to me, it was nice working with it from me, in my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that his diminished responsibility does not cover just one act but could cover a whole series of acts over a period of several months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Then I need to refer to my third report, but the one case I could reconstruct more detailed with Mr. Landzo recently, then I can give for that act, he was diminished responsible. Maybe for the other acts, because he told me more than he could do at January in 1997, because then he didn't tell me anything at all. And now he told me more about how it was in that camp, what he felt in that camp, and he told me about the interpersonal influence and those things. He didn't tell me in January 1996 -- 1997, so, therefore, I can't go a bit further. So I think it is something between, for that special act, I think this diminished responsibility, but I think it counts for the whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: For the whole period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: For any act that Mr. Landzo is alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not any act, but then I need to -- I should have had a possibility to talk with him about the acts, other acts which are mentioned in the indictment, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: But he denied those; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. Is it ever in your experience then concerning Mr. Landzo, then, isn't it true, Doctor, that in his particular case, some of his acts, any activities that he did, may have been the product of complete free will, 100 per cent free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible, but I didn't say -- if I say it is possible, everything in life is possible, so it's not more specific than that as an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: If I may just have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: In the document presented to you by the Defence counsel, there is reference to the personality disorder description in the document, the second document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Concerning guilt, rejection and humiliation as being factors. I don't have the document in front of me, but I believe that was a description of the personality -- one of the facets of the personality disorder mentioned in the document. Under clinical features, are you with me on that one? Do you know where I'm talking about, Doctor? The clinical features of -- from the DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you using any of those clinical features -- do you have the document now and are you looking at the section I'm referring to, the clinical features?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Does that section have any bearing on your diagnosis that you are making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the clinical factors of the post-traumatic stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And you are not finding that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't suppose so because he was still in the situation of stressful circumstances and stressful events, and the post-traumatic stress disorder usually develops afterwards. Therefore, I don't presume at that particular time he could already have developed post-traumatic stress disorder. It came later. You see, therefore, I referred to as the adjustment disorder as a clinical definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You found in 1992, the best you can do is say that he had an adjustment disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a disorder, it means a disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Not post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already from theoretical issues, you must presume that it couldn't yet have been developed at that time, because he was still under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. Just to clarify, these clinical features here, you are not saying that Mr. Landzo exhibited these features?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe a tiny little bit, but it has nothing to do with the concept of the post-traumatic stress disorder, for reasons I explained to you. He was still in the situation of -- you can say this is a definite maladaptation, and this is a situation where you are still under the fire of the stressful circumstances, but you can't adjust your developing symptoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So it's an adjustment disorder then, Doctor, is what you're diagnosis is of Mr. Landzo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the best possible diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. van Leeuwen, the Prosecutor just said to you that the only thing you have diagnosed Mr. Landzo with with regard to his mental state in 1992 is an adjustment disorder, but that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because if you talk about an adjustment disorder, you need always to explain who could develop such an disorder, and then you come to clinical -- to what is maybe the first clinical conclusion, that he has a mixed personality disorder, and especially the borderline and dependent traits are relevant for explaining the interaction with those specific circumstances. And then after that, you can explain how could he develop an adjustment disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The disorders, the personality disorders that you identified under the DMS-IV that Mr. Landzo did suffer in 1992 were schizoid and dependent personality disorders and possibly others. That's what you include in your mixed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the basis is the -- what we call the borderline structure, and the main issue is feeling that you are empty. You don't have a self, and that gives a fair chance that you are conducting with others in a way which is described on the schizoid category, and if you are empty inside, you are very much vulnerable for completely absorbing what's coming from outside, if you get a chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, that borderline type that you're describing is listed on that table, 27-1, from the book that we described earlier, Kaplan and Sadock book, and borderline type is discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, borderline type.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And dependent personality and schizoid personality disorders are all discussed with the criteria on those tables, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecutor also said that it is possible that he was acting under his own free will, but what we are talking about as a psychiatrist, as a clinical psychiatrist, and as a forensic psychiatrist, you answer questions not on what is possible, because you said anything is possible, but you answer questions on reasonable, psychiatric probability, and there is a big difference there, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the Prosecutor asked me is it possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That question I answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't determine --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nothing to do with my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were talking about the adjustment disorder, a personality disorder must have interaction -- there's three factors, I think, personality disorder, then a circumstance of some sort, and then the reaction, the affects on behaviour, and that's what you look at is the whole picture, the three elements, not just one or two, but all three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because that represents more of the reality of a human being than just only describing some traits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, are you leading evidence to show that the acts attributed to him, that he had committed those acts under the direction of anyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, part of his personality disorder has to do with being such a dependent personality that he could not exercise free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what I said. Are you leading to show that he had committed those alleged acts under the direction of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's part of it. That would be one of these personality disorders but he suffers from several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When you are talking of free will, this means that he is acting under the influence of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is part of it and that's one of the reasons that he could not exercise free will. But the Defence releases on other reasons that he couldn't exercise free will also, and I believe it has to do with this mixed disorder, and not just one facet of it. I will ask Dr. van Leeuwen if I'm correct in that, but it's not just one simple dependent personality, it has to do with other facets of the personality disorders that the psychiatrists have evaluated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because in the statement before the psychiatrist, he had named someone as a person who told him to do those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that is part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's why Mr. Moran was very angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I understand that completely, Your Honour. I'm not here with blinders on. I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is an understatement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is there another question that I can help answer the court before I go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are the one who is re-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You talk of free will. You talk that somebody had molded that will or influenced that will, so there has to be evidence that somebody did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is our first witness. We have 27 listed. I will try to bring all of that together as the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just to be aware of this position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was stated in the Pre-trial brief in 1997, so this is not ambush.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to the fact that the Prosecutor asked you about a paragraph on page 15 of your third report. Well, you said it remained unclear whether he suffered from a personality disorder. At that time, you didn't have as much information as you have now. Now today after interviewing Mr. Landzo, you can clearly say that he has a personality disorder, can't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and -- but I warned that I think, and that is vulnerability was clear, was obvious at that time too, yes? But, you know, how do you develop a diagnosis of personality disorder? You need somebody being an adult, and you see how he is developing himself in the adult society, and then you discovery the characteristics of a personality disorder. But when his adulthood started, he was in such extreme circumstances, that I thought at that time it is rather dangerous to make interpretations, because we don't know how he will react in an adult society. And we still don't know, but I got more information, and I think it is very relevant too, clinically relevant, that under the influence of psychotherapy, his condition could improve so much as he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you talk about vulnerability, that is a layman's term or a term that you use as just one facet of describing a dependent personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the key issue or the key characteristic of a personality disorder. Everyone is vulnerable, but if you are suffering from a personality disorder, you are very vulnerable for the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the reason that this kind of personality disorder is different from my personality disorder or Judge Jan's personality disorder is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I don't like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just saying a normal person, if I can characterise myself as normal, would be that theirs is an extreme case and it's pervasive throughout their life. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that you have a lack of capacity to adapt to the way -- to the circumstances which are variable in life. You always react in the same way from your personality disorder, and you can't make choices. Even so, you do things which are not fruitful for you because you need to react in that way. And a mature personality, you can make choices. As I explained to you, a mature personality can make a choice to obey in a system because he likes that or he likes to work, but an immature person is always looking for -- can only obey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to Mr. Moran's cross-examination of you. Mr. Moran alluded to a personality disorder called anti-social. Would you say that Mr. Landzo is suffering from an anti-social personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, definitely not. As I explained, meeting somebody or suffering from that disorder gives you another experience than meeting Mr. Landzo, even earlier. That's first. So I think the key -- the problems on the level of the personality structure which are described with anti-social personality disorder doesn't apply upon the problems in the personality structure of Mr. Landzo. Second, if you reduce your way of thinking to symptoms, yes, or to descriptions, then the correct traits, the virtues, the characteristics of the anti-social personality disorder doesn't apply neither for Mr. Landzo's case history.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, as far as any kind of criminal activity was concerned, none of that was evident in Mr. Landzo before 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I -- anyhow, he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about malingering, because Mr. Moran made it sound like malingering as under anti-social behaviour was the same as telling the truth or not telling the truth. Can you explain to the court the difference between malingering and what the DSM-IV is talking about in that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Malingering is different because you play some kind of illness because you don't want to work anymore. You can have somebody who has the feeling I can't work anymore, because I sleep very badly and I have nightmares and I lost all self-confidence, then he can't work because of a certain kind of disease. But then you have somebody who thinks, life is much easier if I stay home. How can you manage that? You need to go to the doctor and say to the doctor, I can't work, I have this, and I have this and I have this and I have that. Boys and girls who don't like to go to school, and sometimes for a couple of days, they malinger. That's malingering. And if something else, then telling the truth and not telling the truth is another issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As part of your expertise as a forensic psychiatrist and based on all your experience, you're trained to be able to look for the symptoms and the characteristics of someone who is really malingering and someone who is being sincere about their disorders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because usually somebody doesn't know all the factors which are -- usually a disease, you have many symptoms. You have a combination of symptoms, and only if you find that combination then you can conclude, and usually somebody -- he come and tell me this, and he come and tell me that, and he come and tell that, and then I think that's not a combination. That's clinical evidence based upon clinical evidence. So usually it is -- it doesn't occur so often, as you may think, in my work, especially with inmates. Sometimes they try to get out of the system, but it's very easy to be recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to also reoffer the paper that I had earlier talking about personality disorders. That comes directly from Mr. Moran's book which is the bible on DSM-IV by the American Psychiatric Association, page 63. So, if the court would allow me to reoffer that document now, I would like for it to be accepted as authoritative on personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The typed one which is not recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there is one which is in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it's marked D47/4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, D47/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's D47 or D48. It's the one that's type without an identification on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object that on page 63 of the DMS-IV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's page 633.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Page 63 has to do with stuttering.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's page 633 of the DMS-IV manual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have to properly identify the source so it can be admitted into evidence and so where you got it from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's why I'm trying to do that orally in court, that D48/4 is directly from the DSM-IV manual, page 633, and I ask that it be admitted into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. I don't see the problem in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Dr. van Leeuwen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm still not too satisfied with the state of the mental condition of the accused. If I remember rightly, you have rated his mental intelligence as above average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And that he is not retarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't talk about retarded mental capacity, especially if you -- I mean, mental retardation has to do with intelligence and usually we think so. No, I said that a lack of mental capacity, and capacity, that means more, much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, if he is not retarded and he is above average, so he has at least normal mental capacity to commit acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the references I'm used to working with, we say mental retardation has to do with intelligence and mental capacity has to do with all your psychological, all your mental functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Together, everything together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So if you are above average, then you have no such inhibitions as to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you can have shortness in empathy. You can have shortness in capacity to control your impulses. You can have a shortness in social capacities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In law, that does not excuse anybody. Merely because you have no empathy, you can not show emotions of a particular type. That doesn't help you. If your mental capacity is so affected that you have a retardation of your ability to act, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For an act, you need more than intelligence, do you understand? For an act, you need more than intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, physical probability, everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other capacity. We use, what we call, "gebrekkige ontwikkeling," which is an impaired development of your mental capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So originally, last century, it was designed only for intelligence, but later on we use it for your whole mental capacity. And then in your report, you define what capacities -- in what capacities you find a likeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is you referred also to his problems, as you indicated in the diagram, his adjustment of the life, none of these things arose out of any diseases whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, he has a lack of capacity to be an independent adult person. That's a lack of capacity from a clinical point of view, and that is clinically relevant in this case. He has not a lack of intelligence. He has a lack of capacity to be independent, and that we can explain because he has borderline structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are these the factors which enable you to say that he has diminished responsibility for his actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have a shortness, if you lack in capacity to be an independent person, that makes you very vulnerable. And then if you get certain circumstances, then you can get into a condition in which, from a clinical point of view, you can't fully exercise your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can't restrain your passions, do you mean? If you can't reexplain your passions, you are a strong boxer, you can beat up anybody, that should excuse you from any responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because that nothing to do with a mental disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's true. Now, where lies this mental disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I told you. It's on the level of a mixed personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And on the level of the adjustment disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to know your opinion about how the use of power can affect or influence the personality or the behaviour of someone suffering this adjustment disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he is under the influence of power or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: If he has power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How to use his power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that makes an immature person. I'll use in general words, is more dangerous if getting power than a mature person. Do you understand? I think that is very obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question based on that response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That would also depend on what authority figure that a dependent personality would be basing his identity on, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The vulnerability is that you lose the ability to make a choice, to say, "I don't want to follow that person, and I would like to join that person." If somebody is overwhelming, then you take everything. And sometimes a mature person can get into a situation that the situation doesn't allow him to make any choice, but I mean another issue. It is the immaturity of the personality which limits the responsibility to make choices.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. van Leeuwen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your evidence. I think that was very --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very interesting for me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are discharged. Can we have your other witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence is faced with a little logistics problem right now. We have Dr. Verde as our next witness, but I've been informed we don't have an Italian interpreter until tomorrow, and that's with us bringing in an independent Italian interpreter, so I ask the courts indulgence to allow us to start with Dr. Verde in the morning once we get the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But you indicated that you have two or three Dutch specialists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but they are not present in the courtroom because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You were supposed to have them present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: They are not listed in the order to be here present today. I mean, that's not how we scheduled it. The next person in order was Dr. Verde and we don't have the Italian interpreter until the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is he here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Verde is here. He's out in the outer room right now. I mean he's in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you inform them that you needed an Italian interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm not going to place the blame on the registry. On Thursday, we notified the registry that we needed a Dutch interpreter for Dr. Van Leeuwen today but we proceeded without one, but I don't feel that it would be possible to proceed without an Italian interpreter and the registry has informed me that they can't have one here today. If Dr. Verde feels comfortable in speaking -- he speaks English, but I think that with the technical diagnostic explanations that we have, that it would be much better for Dr. Verde to speak in his native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you say that he will be speaking in Italian, this is another unmerited holiday again. I didn't expect this. I thought since you were having a Dutch interpreter, you would utilise the provision for other Dutch witnesses. This is what I expected anybody would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have the Dutch interpreter here either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This gentleman was speaking very good English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, that we went forward with that even without a Dutch interpreter, even though we had requested one, because I felt that Dr. van Leeuwen spoke very good English. But I don't believe that Dr. Haeseker or Dr. Lammers would feel comfortable testifying without a Dutch interpreter, and I don't feel that Dr. Verde would feel comfortable testifying without an Italian interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not too comfortable with this type of arrangement. I want a tidier arrangement when bringing your witnesses. This is a situation you would have known much earlier than now, even telling the registry on Thursday, was very much of an untidy way of arranging it. You knew that it might require other interpreters. These are not the official languages of the Trial Chamber. You should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I filed my final witness list on Thursday and at the same time I requested the interpreters that I foresaw that we needed at that time. If it was untimely, then I apologise to the court, but based on the scheduling that we have done, that's when I requested it. If the court would like, I can try to get victim and witnesses to get one of the Bosnian witnesses here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You didn't think about it? If any other witness comes we substitute him for it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think I am semi-prepared to go ahead and present one of the Bosnian witnesses if we can get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We can break now. You make the arrangements so we'll come back in 30 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry will not have any objection. You can save some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I don't have any objection. I don't anticipate that I would ask for any sort of break, but certainly we can hear them and -- as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It will save us some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You know we have been very flexible about not getting our required notice and going with little notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have half an hour at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just want to inform the court that these were witnesses that have been out in Naaldwijk during the Jazz Festival and I think victim and witnesses may have brought them in by now since the festival is over with, but I will check with them immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I hope they enjoyed the festival.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: They were out in where ever that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will break now and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, yes, you may proceed to call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The Defence calls Senadin Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me first just tell the court that we were fortunate that Victims and Witnesses Unit did have him. Mr. Turkovic was able to be here. The majority of my notes on this witness are in my hotel room. The clerks at the hotel were kind enough to go get them. We have a legal assistant on the way to the Bel Air now. At some point -- is he here? Great. I can go ahead and get started. I was just going to ask the court's indulgence in getting those notes. Would it be easier if I waited about one minute until I got those notes or do you want me to begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Get his name and other particulars in the meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, please state your name for the court?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Senadin Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Please tell us your age, where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of July, 1964 in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What is your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak citizen of the federation, that is, of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, would the court allow me just a minute to shuffle some paper and get my notes out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as luck would have it, I have two notebooks that say "Landzo Defence Witnesses," and I did my best to explain to the receptionist exactly which notebook and what names; however, I'm going to rely on my memory because I was given the wrong book. I would ask the interpreters -- I did explain to Mr. Turkovic a few minutes that I would be getting my notes from our discussion the other day. I would ask that he just be informed of that I don't have those notes, but I do have some notes, and we will do the best that we can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Have you lived in Konjic all of your life?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, ever since my birth, and I'm still living in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: How are you employed?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm working in a state-owned company. I have been working there for 12 to 13 years. This company is based in Celebici, and I also do some private business.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You told me the other day a little bit about that private business. Will you tell the court what other businesses you are involved with?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I also worked in a state-owned company, but I had a private business of my own, that is, a restaurant and a shop, together with a Croatian company as a sales outlet. Now I have a store, which is quite large, rather, a restaurant, with about 200 seats. Next year, I plan to double the capacity. I work with my sister, and privately we do the accounting for several other private companies. I'm also a war veteran, a disabled war veteran, and I was retired as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: At a point a little later in the questioning, I'm going to ask you about that injury. You mentioned that you are a war veteran, and I will be following up on that in just a few minutes, okay?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Are you married, Mr. Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fortunately I am, and I have a child who will soon be one year old.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: In fact, the one-year birthday of this child is the reason that we brought you to testify this week rather than next week; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to 1992. What were you doing before the war began?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I was working in the way that I have just described, that is, I was self-employed as well as working in a public company.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You told me earlier that you had been so employed for 12 or 13 years, so I recall that now.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Eight years until the war, but due to the fact that years of service are doubled during wartime, I have a total of 12 or 13 years of service now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Would you explain to me exactly what was your capacity during the war as in TO, et cetera, whatever you were when you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain whether you are referring to the situation before the war, that is, where I did my military service or now during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll ask you in two parts. What was the first type of military service that you had and how old were you when you had that military service?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service for the first time in Belgrade. I was 18, going on 19, and I was there for 28 (sic) days. I was in a special branch of the army, that is, as a military policeman in Tito's Guard. Do you need any further details about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You told me that you were 18 or 19 and you told me when you were born. About what year did you do this service?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I was 18 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just for my own benefit, do you recall the year that you did this service in Belgrade, like, 1980-something?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: 1983, and I returned in 1984 on the 22nd of July. Actually, I spent 428 days in all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was an error on the part of the interpreter, the number of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: 428, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me now draw your attention -- Your Honours, may I stop and just get some water? Thanks. Let me now draw your attention back to 1992. When do you recall the war starting for you?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: For me, the war started when the people of orthodox religion took to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what month that was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The end of March and the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: At that time, did you become a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What was your position in the TO and what was your function in the TO? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: At first, I was a regular soldier like any other volunteer. In time, I was appointed deputy commander or the leader of the security for the collection centre at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Distance-wise, for my information, about how far from Konjic -- about how far from Celebici to Musala in distance?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be very precise but roughly eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I believe you told me that your position at Musala was as a commander, a coordinator for security, and I believe you told me that you had something to do with scheduling the guards. Could you give me a little bit more of a description of what your job at Musala was?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my duty was to schedule the guards. My main task was to assign the guards who were, at first, members of the TO and, later, of the army in order to provide security for all entrances to the facility where people of orthodox religion were accommodated or, in short, I can call them Serbs. They were placed there so that no one could reach them, either us or citizens or refugees of our own religion who had already been expelled by those same Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sure that the number changed, but approximately could you tell me how many Serbs were in Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: That is a difficult question, but the number varied up to as many as 200, I think. Then later on, the number dropped to about 90, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Since you were in charge of the security at Musala, can you tell me about how many people you were in charge of? About how many people were employed in that capacity at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the total number of people or just the number of people per shift?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Per shift would be a better question.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: There were eight to nine men on the outside per shift, and there were those who were ready. With those, the number went up to about 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did any of the guards spend more time at Musala than just their shift? Were there places to sleep there or did everyone leave Musala at the end of their shift?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Some people stayed to sleep there. There was a special room for that purpose. I couldn't tell you exactly how many beds there were. I know that at times, there were two to a bed to rest on. They had the same food as we did, and they were there in case of need. We could wake them up and call them up to help us should that need arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting Esad Landzo at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When I say "meeting," you didn't know Esad Landzo well before Musala, did you, Mr. Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Esad Landzo before the war, not even his brother, whom I know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me specifically draw your attention now to Esad Landzo and his position at Musala. Do you recall how he came to be hired at Musala? Do you recall the circumstances of his coming to Musala in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I really do not recall the circumstances under which he came, nor do I know where he came from or where he was sent from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall his arriving in Musala about mid to late January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: He came to Musala in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when he left Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: He left Musala maybe ten days after the aggression of the Croats against the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall what month that would have been?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the month of April. It was on the 15th of April that the aggression was carried out against Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That's the date I had as well. Let me ask you to tell me what kind of jobs you assigned Esad Landzo to do at Musala? What were his tasks at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Esad Landzo's tasks at Musala were, in the first place, security for the collection centre at Musala. Some people call it a prison. Others call it a collection centre. Apart from those tasks, Esad Landzo was also required, like all the other people who were members of the security, to provide security of the frontlines towards the Serbs. We regularly had to send reinforcements numbering five to ten soldiers to cover a certain position. I can't remember exactly how many times Esad Landzo went there. When I asked for volunteers, he applied himself, and he went with me to the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When you went to the frontlines, do you recall how long you were there before you came back to Musala prison, the scheduling?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: We would mostly stay two, three, or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Now let me direct the questioning back to your observations of Esad Landzo in Musala. Can you describe for me his behaviour with the Serbs there in Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Would you say that he had a good relationship with the people that he was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the leading that's been going on, that question included.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What were your observations of Esad Landzo's behaviour at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me say that at Musala, while I was the commander or deputy commander of the collection centre at Musala or when I was in charge of the security of the same facility, we warned all soldiers in the unit to respect human rights - Senad Kazagic had required us to do this - so as to avoid any mistreatment, any seizure of property or goods intended for those prisoners, let me call them that. Esad Landzo had no incidents with those people who were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I heard you just say that the standard of treatment for the people at Musala was that there was no mistreatment, no hitting, no pushing, no beating; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Who let everyone know that those were the procedures to be followed at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: We would receive orders from the commander of the Right Bank, Senad Kazagic, and those orders were then passed on by myself and the commander of that facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did you specifically tell Esad Landzo and the other guards that that was the behaviour that you expected of guards at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did Esad Landzo follow this high standard for the treatment of Serbs at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I could say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Would you also say that you never had to discipline Mr. Landzo about -- let me rephrase that. Did he obey the rules at Musala, obey your rules?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, and let me be quite frank, he did violate those rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When he violated this rule, what was your reaction or what was the reaction of someone in authority at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The warden reacted, the warden of the facility. What actually happened, I don't really know because he didn't tell me. So I don't know what disciplinary measure was taken against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me back up just a little bit. You used the term "violation of the rules." Can you tell me what that violation was?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't myself an eyewitness, so I find it difficult to describe it, but I learned from others that he made a movement in the direction of one of the prisoners. Whether he hit him or not, I don't know. This was noticed by the warden who reprimanded him for this. This happened only once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then, in your opinion, that Mr. Landzo, once he was told that that kind of behaviour did not take place at Musala, did he follow the rules from then on out?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. She's leading the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall if this violation occurred when Mr. Landzo first came to Musala?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. She's leading the witness again. I have no objection if she wants to ask, "When, if you know, did this incident happen," but this continued leading I do object to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, if you know, when did this violation of the rules at Musala occur?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you the exact date. I know it was at the beginning, maybe a month or a month and a half after the facility was established as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Once Mr. Landzo was instructed by the authorities there not to behave that way, did he then behave accordingly?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I told you that I would go back to the injury that you received on the frontlines. Let me ask you, please, to tell the court about that injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it really relevant for our purposes? You're leading evidence with regard to Musala. We're interested with Celebici. He may be a very good person before joining Celebici. He may be a very good person after he left Celebici. We're concerned with specific allegations against him in regards to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you leading evidence of his good conduct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you leading evidence of his good conduct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Am I looking for evidence of his good conduct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because then if the Prosecution will be able to show that he was not a person of good conduct, how can it help you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I think I'm working towards a contrast to show how his dependent personality molded to the different type of authority figure at Musala, and that was the point of my line of questioning. When the leadership demanded a certain behaviour at Musala, that he was able to follow that. That was the point of those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is his injury really relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I can move on. May I just have about 30 seconds?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention back to the frontline, not to ask about your injury, but to ask about Esad Landzo's behaviour on the frontlines. Would you characterise him as a good soldier, as an obedient soldier?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, again, to her leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What type of soldier would you describe Esad Landzo to be when you observed him on the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Esad Landzo, I would say, was much better than some other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That doesn't amount to much.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: On the frontline, he always volunteered when I asked for volunteers. He was a man who wanted action, who wasn't afraid of being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did he follow the orders of the people in authority on the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He volunteered when he was always asked to do things. When everyone was asked, he volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Then that would imply that he followed orders from the authority figures when he was on the frontlines? Let me move on. I think I have covered that. Were you aware of a hand injury or a disability to Mr. Landzo's hand? If you're not aware of it, just tell me so.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of a hand injury sustained before the war, by Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said that I didn't know Esad Landzo before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that. Were you aware of any type of hand injury that you would have -- did you notice any hand disability when Mr. Landzo was at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, it was a war, and nobody heeded any injuries. Even if he had no leg, if he could carry a weapon, he would have been used and he would have had to fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recognise Mr. Landzo in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised him with difficulty but I did recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: May I ask you to expand on that? What is the difficulty that you had today in recognising Mr. Landzo? What's the difference between Mr. Landzo today and when you knew him at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The first difference that I can observe is his haircut. His hair is longer and he is much heavier. His face is fuller. He looks like a gentleman, a bit like a gentleman. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, were you with Esad Landzo at Glavaticevo, were you with him in that area of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the place? I didn't understand the name of the place you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if I could just be of assistance. I think the name was Glavaticevo. Does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we all had the same problem. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's get the interpretation through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Moran did not switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: None of us heard any interpretation on the last statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The translation did not come through. Maybe there's something wrong with the translation booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I hear it will take some five minutes to correct it. Okay, we can rise for five minutes and come back at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me go back to one of the things that we discussed before the break. We had discussed briefly that --

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Back to the incident that you discussed earlier about Mr. Landzo gesturing to a prisoner and being protected by someone in authority. I believe you said you weren't there right at the time. Did you walk in directly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The warden of the facility came, and later I reprimanded Landzo, and then the warden punished him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did the warden tell you what had happened?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Other soldiers told me that he raised his hand and he moved his hand aside, whether he hit him, whether he tried to hit him, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you of any injury as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose injury are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that. You say that it was a gesture and that he moved his hand toward a prisoner; is that what you're saying happened?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he moved his hand. Whether he hit him or not, I can't tell you. Whether he wanted to hit him or just push him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: But the people that told you this, did they tell you there was a hit or did they tell you that you just raised his hand?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He answered that. He said that he was punished for his conduct. I think that should have satisfied you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a policy at Musala wherein Serbs were allowed to leave the prison to go do some types of work. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were allowed to go out. Some were allowed to go home. They were escorted by guards to have a bath because we didn't want to have an epidemic. They have the same toilet facilities as we did. Some of them went to work in the hospital. They got better food. They had their own cook there. In the clinic of Konjic, they volunteered for them, about a dozen of them. And then they also carried coal. They also peeled potatoes and did similar kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When you say they were escorted, did Esad Landzo on occasion escort these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember it. I can't tell you precisely. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall a Serb at Musala -- I'll try to get this right, whose name was Mico Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Mico Kuljanin, a fat fellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to observe the way Mr. Kuljanin and Mr. Landzo interreacted (sic) or -- that's a bad word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Related to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. How was Mico Kuljanin treated at Musala? Did he have some special treatment at Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was subjected to no particular treatment. He even had some privileges compared to other inmates. He was even allowed to go to town. He was married in Konjic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When you say he was married in Konjic at that time, not during his confinement at Musala, but before he came to Musala; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was an inmate in Musala, a detainee in Musala. In 1993, he was discharged from Musala. He remained in Konjic. He joined the army. He married a girl and he has a son, and he still works in Konjic. He is a successful businessman. He has two companies now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention back to when Mr. Kuljanin was at Musala. If Mr. Kuljanin came to this Tribunal and testified that he was mistreated at Musala, he would not be telling the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I came here and I swore I would tell the truth. I would tell Mr. Kuljanin, if he said so, that he is lying. I would say it openly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: In your capacity as head of security at Musala, you never saw anybody beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in my presence, and if it had happened when I was not present there, the Serbs who were there, who were detained, some of whom who were my friends, they would have told me. Q.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your minutes are accumulating.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This will be the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, are you familiar with a Bendzo Dusko who attempted to leave Musala prison, to escape from Musala?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dusko Bendzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask about the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Bendzo is in the indictment and I think it's very relevant that this testimony comes out now, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's related to his period in Musala prison, apparently.

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I know several Bendzo. If you gave me his photograph, I could describe him. If he showed me a photograph, there is one who is called Dusan Bendzo. Could you tell me what he looks like, how tall he is, what his hair looks like? Could you give me a description of that person?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All I can tell you, I can't tell you a physical description, but I can tell you that he did try to escape from Musala, if that helps you to remember?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help me when it was, what year? Was it in 1992 or at the beginning of '93?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I don't know. So I'm not going to be able to help you with that. I have information that it was in 1993 or 1994 and that he was a former taxi driver who escaped from --

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know the gentleman. I think that he even managed to escape. That was in 1994 after the surrender by the army of the facility of the military police. I think that this fact is true, but I don't know the details. I know that taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Were you there at Musala when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am still going to object to relevancy, whether or not someone who is mistreated in Celebici subsequently escaped from Musala, we believe, is totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I only ask it because it was part of the indictment and I thought this witness might be able to give us a little more information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly there's nothing in the indictment about any escape from Musala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which count is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I may just have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might assist, it's in the count alleging tortures under command responsibility, and what it would show is that -- I believe that the evidence would be that Mr. Bendzo escaped and killed the guard at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He admitted that himself in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He didn't come to testify, Mr. Bendzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Somebody did come and say that he escaped, he wasn't exchanged and he had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But Mr. Bendzo never came in the Prosecution's case. That's why I was asking the question, because he is still in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's Count 38, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't have my indictment in front of me, Your Honour, but it's the one -- general charges under command responsibility, I believe, for torture.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And if I might just clarify, in addition to him not testifying, I believe there was testimony that from one witness who indicated that some persons escaped, and he said absolutely no one was injured, no guards were injured at that time, and he couldn't say what happened after that, just to, I think, clarify the record. In any event, we believe subsequent events about Musala are totally irrelevant to whether or not he was mistreated in Celebici, unless they are going to suggest that somehow he was tortured in Celebici because someone thought that a year later he was going to escape from Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I don't think that was the point of -- the point of questions and bringing this witness to testify about Musala was just to kind of move forward from the testimony from Dr. van Leeuwen this morning about his dependent personality and how he was able to adapt to whatever authority figure was in his life at the time. That was the point of bringing this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you still have anything to ask him, then move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I pass the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: With your handicap, you couldn't do much. Was there any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I assure the court that for my next witness, I'll be much better prepared than this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of questions. I can probably do it in five minutes, if you will give me that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have any questions, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Defence counsel have to set the order, I move that my colleague Mr. Moran has the first question. We agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic, and I want to ask you about four questions based on what you testified to on your direct. I'm going to go from back to front. The last question that Ms. Boller asked you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. The witness got the same translation and the translation said that Mr. Moran represented Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Since the transcript doesn't say so, the witness heard the same thing as I did. Mr. Moran does not represent Mr. Delalic. Could we get the right translation so that we don't confuse the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I represent Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I didn't hear the correction. Okay, I have seen it here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The last question that you were asked about Dusko Bendzo reminded me to ask you a question about a man by the name of Risto Vukalo. Did you ever hear of, see, engage in any mock executions at the Musala prison to scare prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: At Musala, there were no executions during the year while I was in charge of security. That I can allege emphatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about a mock execution where you scare somebody, you make him think you are going to execute him but you don't do it. Maybe you fire over his head, something like that. Did any of that occur?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: In my presence, such an event never occurred. I mentioned that I spent several days on the frontlines on seven or eight occasions, but somebody would have told me, because this can provoke a great deal of fear and this can affect a person's health. He can have a heart attack or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, were prisoners or detainees, I guess is the right word, from Musala ever taken to the frontlines and forced to dig trenches or things like that -- create fortifications for the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single Serb prisoner built fortifications for the army. They did carry food, but they would select people from amongst themselves to do this. They selected the persons themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me go on to another subject. You said that some of the Serb detainees were allowed to go home -- excuse me, to have a bath because you did not want an epidemic. Do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kind of epidemic are we talking about and why did you fear it?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: We were afraid of hepatitis; we were afraid of other infections, because, after all, there were quite a large number of people in a group, many soldiers. This was all interconnected. It could affect their families, our families. The pressure in the water pipes was low, so there was a shortage of water. We had one large room for these purposes, and if people didn't wash regularly, then, of course, infections could spread, especially in the summer months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So based on medical advice, you allowed these people to go wherever they could to take showers so they could be clean to prevent epidemics; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: This was even contrary to the orders of the commanders. This was the decision taken by the warden and myself. I personally took some people, escorted some people, on a number of occasions. I can even give you some names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but what I'm asking is you did this based on medical advice to prevent epidemic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The doctors came regularly and they told us that that is what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine, that's what I was getting at, sir. The next thing I would like to ask you about, and, again, I'm changing subjects completely. You testified about an incident where Mr. Landzo supposedly raised a hand in the direction of a detainee. Without getting into the facts of that incident at all, as I recall, you testified that you reprimanded Mr. Landzo which, in my army would be, you chewed him out, and he was later punished by the warden. Was that because, as the deputy commander, you lacked the authority to punish?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I could have punished him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You referred to Musala as a collection centre, as opposed to a prison. Was that a place where people who were not suspected of committing crimes against the government were taken to be protected? Is that what Musala was for?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a rather complicated question. Every prisoner in that collection centre was arrested with a firearm on him, so he was a prisoner, after all, but he was set aside there because we wanted to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Protect them and protect the government also from people with guns?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how one could put it, because they had the same food as I did. There was no difference between the Bosnian soldier and this arrested Serb with a gun in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, by the way, when were you assigned to Musala? I heard that and then I just didn't put it down in my notes. When were you first assigned there as the commander of the guard?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to tell you the exact date. Maybe one of the gentlemen could help. After the arrival of a group of soldiers who were transferred from Celebici, I was assigned by Mr. Senad Kazazic to another facility intended for military purposes, but as there were fewer guards than was necessary, Mr. Kazazic then transferred me to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't need an exact date. Was it April or May or June?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: It was June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were there, were there any prisoners who were transferred from Celebici to Musala?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a large number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When they came in, did they look beaten, starved, kicked, abused?

utterances.speaker: SENADIN TURKOVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't notice very much on them. Of course, they were all dirty because none of their people had any clothing, enough clothing, to send them. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think you better do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You better do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think I'll quit while I'm ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is this Ms. McHenry cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We will certainly be cross-examining this witness, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I wasn't sure if even other Defence counsel wanted to do it, but we definitely would like to cross-examine and I'm ready to start at Your Honours' convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, are you cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
